sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: I will conclude briefly —

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Hold your peace, you roaring rascal, I’ll run my head i’your chaps else. [To Cokes] You were best build a booth and entertain him, make your will, an you say the word, and him your heir! Heart, I never knew one taken with a mouth of a peck afore. By this light, I’ll carry you away o’my back, an you will not come.

div2.stage: He gets him up on pickpack.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Stay, Numps, stay, set me down: I ha’ lost my purse, Numps. Oh, my purse! One o’my fine purses is gone.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Is’t indeed, brother?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Ay, as I am an honest man, would I were an arrant rogue else! A plague of all roguy, damned cutpurses for me!

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Bless ’em with all my heart, with all my heart, do you see! Now, as I am no infidel that I know of, I am glad on’t. Ay, I am — here’s my witness! — do you see, sir? I did not tell you of his fables, I? No, no, I am a dull malt-horse, I, I know nothing. Are you not justly served i’your conscience now? Speak, i’your conscience. Much good do you, with all my heart, and his good heart that has it, with all my heart again.

p.seg: This fellow is very charitable — would he had a purse too! But I must not be too bold all at a time.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Nay, Numps, it is not my best purse.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Not your best! Death! Why should it be your worst? Why should it be any, indeed, at all? Answer me to that, gi’ me a reason from you why it should be any?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Nor my gold, Numps — I ha’ that yet, look here else, sister.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why so, there’s all the feeling he has!

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: I pray you, have a better care of that, brother.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Nay, so I will, I warrant you; let him catch this, that catch can. I would fain see him get this, look you here.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: So, so, so, so, so, so, so, so! Very good.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I would ha’ him come again now, and but offer at it. Sister, will you take notice of a good jest? I will put it just where th’other was, and if we ha’ good luck, you shall see a delicate fine trap to catch the cutpurse nibbling.

p.seg: Faith, and he’ll try ere you be out o’the Fair.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Come, Mistress Grace, prithee, be not melancholy for my mischance: sorrow wi’ not keep it, sweetheart.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: I do not think on’t, sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ’Twas but a little scurvy white money, hang it — it may hang the cutpurse one day. I ha’ gold left to gi’ thee a fairing yet, as hard as the world goes. Nothing angers me but that nobody here looked like a cutpurse, unless ’twere Numps.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: How? I? I look like a cutpurse? Death! Your sister’s a cutpurse! and your mother and father, and all your kin were cutpurses! And here is a rogue is the bawd o’the cutpurses, whom I will beat to begin with.

div2.stage: They speak all together, and Wasp beats the Justice.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Hold thy hand, child of wrath and heir of anger, make it not Childermas day in thy fury, or the feast of the French Barthol’mew, parent of the Massacre! Massacre! In Creaser’s edition this speech by Justice is printed in a right-hand column alongside the following speeches by Cokes, Mrs Overdo and Wasp.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Numps, Numps!

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Good Master Humphrey!

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: You are the patrico, are you? The patriarch of the cutpurses? You share, sir, they say: let them share this with you. Are you i’your hot fit of preaching again? I’ll cool you!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Murder, murder, murder!

div2.stage: [Enter] WHIT, HAGGIS, [and] BRISTLE. LEATHERHEAD [and] TRASH [return to their wares].

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Nay, ’tish all gone now! Dish ’tish, phen tou vilt not be phitin call, Master Offisher. Phat ish a man te better to lishen out noishes for tee, an tou art in an oder ’orld, being very shuffishient noishes, and gallantsh, too? One o’their brabblesh would have fed ush all dish fortnight. But tou art so bushy about beggarsh still, tou hast no leshure to intend shentlemen, an’t be.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: Why, I told you, Davy Bristle.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Come, come, you told me a pudding, Toby Haggis, a matter of nothing — I am sure it came to nothing! You said, let’s go to Urs’la’s, indeed, but then you met the man with the monsters, and I could not get you from him. An old fool, not leave seeing yet? HAGGIS Why, who would ha’ thought anybody would ha’ quarrelled so early, or that the ale o’the Fair would ha’ been up so soon?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Phy? Phat a’clock toest tou tink it ish, man?

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: I cannot tell.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Tou art a vishe vatchman, i’te meanteeme.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: Why? Should the watch go by the clock, or the clock by the watch, I pray?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: One should go by another, if they did well.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Tou art right now! Phen did’st tou ever know or hear of a shuffishient vatchman but he did tell the clock, phat bushiness soever he had?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Nay, that’s most true, a sufficient watchman knows what a’clock it is.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Shleeping or vaking! Ash well as te clock himshelf, or te jack dat shtrikes him!

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Let’s inquire of Master Leatherhead or Joan Trash here. — Master Leatherhead, do you hear, Master Leatherhead?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: If it be a Ledderhead, ’tish a very tick Ledderhead, tat sho mush noish vill not piersh him.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: I have a little business now: good friends, do not trouble me.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Phat? Because o’ty wrought neetcap, and ty phelvet sherkin, man? Phy, I have sheen tee in ty ledder sherkin ere now, Mashter o’ de Hobby-horses, as bushy and as stately as tou sheem’st to be.

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Why, what an you have, Captain Whit? He has his choice of jerkins, you may see by that, and his caps too, I assure you, when he pleases to be either sick or employed.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: God-a-mercy Joan, answer for me.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: [To the Watchmen] Away, be not sheen i’my company: here be shentlemen and men of vorship.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: We had wonderful ill luck to miss this prologue o’the purse, but the best is, we shall have five acts of him ere night. He’ll be spectacle enough! I’ll answer for’t.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: O Creesh! Duke Quarlous, how dosht tou? Tou dosht not know me, I fear? I am te vishesht man, but Justish Overdo, in all Barthol’mew Fair now. Gi’ me twelvepence from tee, I vill help tee to a vife vorth forty marks for’t, an’t be.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Away, rogue, pimp, away!

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: And she shall show tee as fine cut-’ork for’t in her shmock, too, as tou cansht vish, i’faith. Vilt tou have her, vorshipful Vinvife? I vill help tee to her here, be ant be, in te pig-quarter: gi’ me ty twel’pence from tee.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Why, there’s twel’pence: pray thee, wilt thou be gone?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Tou art a vorthy man and a vorshipful man still.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Get you gone, rascal.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: I do mean it, man. Prinsh Quarlous, if tou hasht need on me, tou shalt find me here, at Urs’la’s. I vill see phat ale and punk ish i’te pigshty for tee, bless ty good vorship.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Look who comes here! John Littlewit!

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: And his wife, and my widow, her mother: the whole family.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slight, you must gi’ ’em all fairings now!

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Not I, I’ll not see ’em.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: They are going a-feasting. What schoolmaster’s that, is with ’em?

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: That’s my rival, I believe, the baker!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: So, walk on in the middle way, foreright; turn neither to the right hand nor to the left; let not your eyes be drawn aside with vanity nor your ear with noises.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Oh, I know him by that start!

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: What do you lack? What do you buy, pretty mistress? A fine hobby-horse, to make your son a tilter? A drum, to make him a soldier? A fiddle, to make him a reveller? What is’t you lack? Little dogs for your daughters? Or babies, male or female?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Look not toward them, hearken not: the place is Smithfield, or the field of smiths, the grove of hobby-horses and trinkets; the wares are the wares of devils. And the whole Fair is the shop of Satan! They are hooks and baits, very baits, that are hung out on every side to catch you, and to hold you as it were by the gills and by the nostrils, as the fisher doth: therefore, you must not look nor turn toward them — The heathen man could stop his ears with wax against the harlot o’the sea: do you the like with your fingers against the bells of the Beast.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [To Quarlous] What flashes comes from him!

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Oh, he has those of his oven! A notable hot baker ’twas, when he plied the peel. He is leading his flock into the Fair now.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Rather driving ’em to the pens, for he will let ’em look upon nothing.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Gentlewomen, the weather’s hot! Whither walk you? Have a care o’your fine velvet caps, the Fair is dusty. Take a sweet delicate booth, with boughs, here i’the way, and cool yourselves i’the shade — you and your friends. (Littlewit is gazing at the sign, which is the pig’s head with a large writing under it.) The best pig and bottle-ale i’the Fair, sir. Old Urs’la is cook, there you may read: the pig’s head speaks it. Poor soul, she has had a stringhalt, the maryhinchco, but she’s prettily amended.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: A delicate show-pig, little mistress, with shweet sauce, and crackling, like de bay-leaf i’ de fire, la! Tou shalt ha’ de clean side o’ de table-clot and di glass vashed with phatersh of Dame Annessh Clear.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: This’s fine, verily: ‘Here be the best pigs, and she does roast ’em as well as ever she did’, the pig’s head says.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Excellent, excellent, mistress, with fire o’ juniper and rosemary branches! [To John] The oracle of the pig’s head, that, sir.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Son, were you not warned of the vanity of the eye? Have you forgot the wholesome admonition so soon?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Good mother, how shall we find a pig, if we do not look about for’t? Will it run off o’the spit into our mouths, think you, as in Lubberland, and cry, ‘Wee, wee’?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: No, but your mother, religiously wise, conceiveth it may offer itself by other means to the sense, as by way of steam, which I think it doth, here in this place — huh! huh! — yes, it doth. (Busy scents after it like a hound.) And it were a sin of obstinacy, great obstinacy, high and horrible obstinacy, to decline or resist the good titillation of the famelic sense, which is the smell. Therefore be bold — huh! huh! huh! — follow the scent. Enter the tents of the unclean for once, and satisfy your wife’s frailty. Let your frail wife be satisfied; your zealous mother, and my suffering self, will also be satisfied.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Come, Win, as good winny here as go farther and see nothing.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: We scape so much of the other vanities by our early entering.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: It is an edifying consideration.

p.seg: This is scurvy, that we must come into the Fair and not look on’t.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Win, have patience, Win, I’ll tell you more anon.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Mooncalf, entertain within there! The best pig i’the booth, a pork-like pig! These are Banbury-bloods, o’the sincere stud, come a-pig-hunting. Whit, wait, Whit, look to your charge.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: A pig prepare presently, let a pig be prepared to us.

div2.stage: [Exit Whit, guiding Busy, Mistress Purecraft, John, and Win into the booth.]

sp.speaker: MOONCALF
sp.p: ’Slight, who be these?

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Is this the good service, Jordan, you’d do me?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Why, Urs? Why, Urs? Thou’lt ha’ vapours i’thy leg again presently; pray thee, go in: ’t may turn to the scratches else.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Hang your vapours, they are stale, and stink like you. Are these theguests o’the game you promised to fill my pit withal today?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Ay, what ail they, Urs?

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Ail they? They are all sippers, sippers o’the city: they look as they would not drink off two penn’orth of bottle-ale amongst ’em.

sp.speaker: MOONCALF
sp.p: A body may read that i’their small printed ruffs.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Away, thou art a fool, Urs, and thy Mooncalf, too, i’your ignorant vapours now! Hence! Good guests, I say, right hypocrites, good gluttons. In, and set a couple o’ pigs o’the board, and half a dozen of the biggest bottles afore ’em, and call Whit. [Exit Mooncalf into the booth.] I do not love to hear innocents abused: fine ambling hypocrites! And a stone-puritan, with a sorrel head and beard, good-mouthed gluttons — two to a pig. Away!

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Are you sure they are such?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: O’the right breed, thou shalt try ’em by the teeth, Urs. Where’s this Whit?

l.emph: Behold, man, and see, what a worthy man am ee!
With the fury of my sword, and the shaking of my beard,
I will make ten thousand men afeared.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Well said, brave Whit! In, and fear the ale out o’the bottles into the bellies of the Brethren and the Sisters. Drink to the Cause and pure vapours.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Whit and Knockem into the booth.]

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: My roarer is turned tapster, methinks. Now were a fine time for thee, Winwife, to lay aboard thy widow — thou’lt never be master of a better season or place. She that will venture herself into the Fair, and a pig-box, will admit any assault, be assured of that.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: I love not enterprises of that suddenness, though.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: I’ll warrant thee then, no wife out o’the widows’ hundred. If I had but as much title to her as to have breathed once on that strait stomacher of hers, I would now assure myself to carry her yet, ere she went out of Smithfield. Or she should carry me, which were the fitter sight, I confess. But you are a modest undertaker, by circumstances and degrees. Come, ’tis disease in thee, not judgement — I should offer at all together. Look, here’s the poor fool again that was stung by the wasp erewhile.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: I will make no more orations, shall draw on these tragical conclusions. And I begin now to think that, by a spice of collateral justice, Adam Overdo deserved this beating; for I, the said Adam, was one cause (a by-cause) why the purse was lost — and my wife’s brother’s purse, too — which they know not of yet. But I shall make very good mirth with it at supper — that will be the sport — and put my little friend Master Humphrey Wasp’s choler quite out of countenance: when, sitting at the upper end o’my table, as I use, and drinking to my brother Cokes and Mistress Alice Overdo, as I will, my wife, for their good affection to old Bradley, I deliver to ’em it was I that was cudgelled, and show ’em the marks. To see what bad events may peep out o’the tail of good purposes! The care I had of that civil young man I took fancy to this morning (and have not left it yet) drew me to that exhortation; which drew the company, indeed; which drew the cutpurse; which drew the money; which drew my brother Cokes his loss; which drew on Wasp’s anger; which drew on my beating — a pretty gradation! And they shall ha’ it i’their dish, i’faith, at night for fruit — I love to be merry at my table. I had thought once, at one special blow he ga’ me, to have revealed myself! But then (I thank thee, fortitude!) I remembered that a wise man ( and who is ever so great a part o’the commonwealth in himself) for no particular disaster ought to abandon a public good design. The husbandman ought not, for one unthankful year, to forsake the plough; the shepherd ought not, for one scabbed sheep, to throw by his tar-box; the pilot ought not, for one leak i’the poop, to quit the helm; nor the alderman ought not, for one custard more at a meal, to give up his cloak; the constable ought not to break his staff and forswear the watch, for one roaring night; nor the piper o’the parish — ut parvis componere magna solebam — to put up his pipes, for one rainy Sunday. These are certain knocking conclusions: out of which I am resolved, come what come can, come beating, come imprisonment, come infamy, come banishment, nay, come the rack, come the hurdle — welcome all! — I will not discover who I am till my due time; and yet still, all shall be, as I said ever, in justice’ name, and the King’s, and for the commonwealth.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: What does he talk to himself, and act so seriously? Poor fool!

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: No matter what. Here’s fresher argument: intend that.

div2.stage: [Enter] COKES, Mistress OVERDO, [and] GRACE, [followed by] WASP [loaded with purchases]

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Come, Mistress Grace, come, sister, here’s more fine sights yet, i’faith. God’s lid, where’s Numps? LEATHERHEAD What do you lack, gentlemen? What is’t you buy? Fine rattles? Drums? Babies? Little dogs? And birds for ladies? What do you lack?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Good honest Numps, keep afore: I am so afraid thou’lt lose somewhat — my heart was at my mouth when I missed thee.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: You were best buy a whip i’your hand to drive me.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Nay, do not mistake, Numps, thou art so apt to mistake — I would butwatch the goods. Look you now, the treble fiddle was e’en almost like to be lost!

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Pray you, take heed you lose not yourself: your best way were e’en get up and ride for more surety. Buy a token’s worth of great pins to fasten yourself to my shoulder. LEATHERHEAD What do you lack, gentlemen? Fine purses, pouches, pin-cases, pipes? What is’t you lack? A pair o’ smiths to wake you i’the morning? Or a fine whistling bird?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Numps, here be finer things than any we ha’ bought, by odds! And more delicate horses, a great deal! Good Numps, stay, and come hither.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Will you scorse with him? You are in Smithfield, you may fit yourself with a fine easy-going street-nag for your saddle again’ Michaelmas Term, do. Has he ne’er a little odd cart for you to make a caroche on i’the country, with four pied hobby-horses? Why the measles should you stand here with your train, cheaping of dogs, birds, and babies? You ha’ no children to bestow ’em on, ha’ you?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: No, but again’ I ha’ children, Numps, that’s all one.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Do, do, do, do: how many shall you have, think you? An I were as you, I’d buy for all my tenants, too: they are a kind o’ civil savages, that will part with their children for rattles, pipes, and knives. You were best buy a hatchet or two, and truck with ’em.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Good Numps, hold that little tongue o’thine, and save it a labour. I am resolute Bat, thou know’st.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: A resolute fool, you are, I know, and a very sufficient coxcomb, with all my heart! Nay, you have it, sir, an you be angry: turd i’your teeth, twice (if I said it not once afore) and much good do you.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [To Quarlous] Was there ever such a self-affliction? And so impertinent?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Alas! His care will go near to crack him; let’s in, and comfort him.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Would I had been set i’the ground, all but the head on me, and had my brains bowled at or threshed out, when first I underwent this plague of a charge!

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: How now, Numps! Almost tired i’your protectorship? Overparted? Overparted?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why, I cannot tell, sir, it may be I am. Does’t grieve you?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: No, I swear does’t not, Numps: to satisfy you.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Numps? ’Sblood, you are fine and familiar! How long ha’ we been acquainted, I pray you?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: I think it may be remembered, Numps, that! ’Twas since morning, sure.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why, I hope I know’t well enough, sir. I did not ask to be told.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: No? Why then?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: It’s no matter why. You see with your eyes now what I said to you today? You’ll believe me another time?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Are you removing the Fair, Numps?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: A pretty question! and a very civil one! Yes, faith, I ha’ my lading, you see, or shall have anon: you may know whose beast I am by my burden. If the pannier-man’s jack were ever better known by his loins of mutton, I’ll be flayed and feed dogs for him, when his time comes.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [To Quarlous] How melancholy Mistress Grace is yonder! Pray thee, let’s go enter ourselves in ‘ grace’ with her.

div2.stage: [They draw her aside and talk apart with her.]

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: [To Leatherhead] Those six horses, friend, I’ll have —

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: And the three Jews’ trumps; and half-a-dozen o’ birds, and that drum (I have one drum already) and your smiths — I like that device o’your smiths very pretty well. And four halberds — and (le’ me see) that fine painted great lady, and her three women for state, I’ll have.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: No, the shop; buy the whole shop, it will be best, the shop, the shop! LEATHERHEAD If his worship please.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Yes, and keep it during the Fair, bob-chin.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Peace, Numps. [To Leatherhead] Friend, do not meddle with him, an you be wise, and would show your head above board; he will sting thorough your wrought nightcap, believe me. A set of these violins I would buy, too, for a delicate young noise I have i’the country that are every one a size less than another, just like your fiddles. I would fain have a fine young masque at my marriage, now I think on’t — but I do want such a number o’things. And Numps will not help me now, and I dare not speak to him.

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Will your worship buy any gingerbread, very good bread, comfortable bread?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Gingerbread! Yes, let’s see.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: There’s the t’other springe!

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Is this well, Goody Joan? To interrupt my market, in the midst, and call away my customers? Can you answer this at the Piepowders?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Why, if his mastership have a mind to buy, I hope my ware lies as open as another’s: I may show my ware, as well as you yours.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Hold your peace; I’ll content you both: I’ll buy up his shop, and thy basket.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Will you, i’faith?

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Why should you put him from it, friend?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Cry you mercy! You’d be sold too, would you? What’s the price on you, jerkin and all as you stand? Ha’ you any qualities?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Yes, Goodman Angry-man, you shall find he has qualities, if you cheapen him.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: God’s so, you ha’ the selling of him! What are they? Will they be bought for love or money?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: No, indeed, sir.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: For what then? Victuals?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: He scorns victuals, sir, he has bread and butter at home, thanks be to God! And yet he will do more for a good meal, if the toy take him i’the belly — marry then, they must not set him at lower end; if they do, he’ll go away, though he fast. But put him atop o’the table, where his place is, and he’ll do you forty fine things. He has not been sent for and sought out for nothing at your great city-suppers, to put down Coryate and Cokeley, and been laughed at for his labour; he’ll play you all the puppets i’the town over, and the players, every company, and his own company too: he spares nobody!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I’faith?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: He was the first, sir, that ever baited the fellow i’the bear’s skin, an’t like your worship: no dog ever came near him since. And for fine motions!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Is he good at those, too? Can he set out a masque, trow?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: O Lord, master! Sought to far and near for his inventions. And he engrosses all, he makes all the puppets i’the Fair.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Dost thou, in troth, old velvet jerkin? Give me thy hand.

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Nay, sir, you shall see him in his new velvet jerkin, and a scarf, too, at night, when you hear him interpret Master Littlewit’s motion.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Speak no more, but shut up shop presently, friend. I’ll buy both it and thee, too, to carry down with me, and her hamper beside. Thy shop shall furnish out the masque and hers the banquet: I cannot go less to set out anything with credit. What’s the price, at a word, o’thy whole shop, case and all, as it stands?

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Sir, it stands me in six-and-twenty shillings sevenpence halfpenny, besides three shillings for my ground.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well, thirty shillings will do all, then! And what comes yours to?

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Four shillings and eleven pence, sir, ground and all, an’t like your worship.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Yes, it does like my worship very well, poor woman. That’s five shillings more. [He counts out the money to them in turn.] What a masque shall I furnish out for forty shillings — twenty pound Scotch — and a banquet of gingerbread! There’s a stately thing! Numps! Sister! And my wedding gloves too — that I never thought on afore! All my wedding gloves, gingerbread! Oh, me! What a device will there be, to make ’em eat their fingers’ ends! And delicate brooches for the bridemen, and all! And then I’ll ha’ this posy put to ’em: ‘For the best grace’, meaning Mistress Grace, my wedding posy.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: I am beholden to you, sir, and to your Barthol’mew-wit.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: You do not mean this, do you? Is this your first purchase?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Yes, faith, and I do not think, Numps, but thou’lt say it was the wisest act that ever I did in my wardship.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Like enough! I shall say anything, I!

p.seg: I cannot beget a project, with all my political brain, yet; my project is how to fetch off this proper young man from his debauched company. I have followed him all the Fair over, and still I find him with this songster. And I begin shrewdly to suspect their familiarity, and the young man of a terrible taint: poetry! — with which idle disease if he be infected, there’s no hope of him, in a state-course. Actum est of him for a commonwealth’s-man, if he go to’t in rhyme, once.
Yonder he is buying o’ gingerbread: set in quickly, before he part with too much on his money.

lg.l: [sings] My masters and friends and good people, draw near, etc.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Ballads! Hark, hark! (He runs to the ballad man.) Pray thee, fellow, stay a little. — Good Numps, look to the goods. — What ballads hast thou? Let me see, let me see myself.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: [To Quarlous and Winwife] Why so! He’s flown to another lime-bush; there he will flutter as long more, till he ha’ ne’er a feather left. Is there a vexation like this, gentlemen? Will you believe me now? Hereafter shall I have credit with you?

p.seg: I never saw a young pimp-errant and his squire better matched.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Faith, the sister comes after ’em well, too.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Nay, if you saw the Justice her husband, my guardian, you were fitted for the mess. He is such a wise one his way —

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: I wonder we see him not here.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Oh! He is too serious for this place, and yet better sport than the other three, I assure you, gentlemen, where’er he is, though ’t be o’the Bench.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: How dost thou call it? A Caveat against Cutpurses ! — a good jest, i’faith. I would fain see that demon, your cutpurse you talk of, that delicate-handed devil. They say he walks hereabout — I would see him walk now. Look you, sister, here, here, let him come, sister, and welcome. (He shows his purse boastingly.) Ballad man, does any cutpurses haunt hereabout? Pray thee, raise me one or two; begin, and show me one.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: Sir, this is a spell against ’em, spick-and-span new, and ’tis made as ’twere in mine own person, and I sing it in mine own defence. But ’twill cost a penny alone, if you buy it.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: No matter for the price, thou dost not know me, I see — I am an odd Barthol’mew.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Has’t a fine picture, brother?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Oh, sister, do you remember the ballads o’er the nursery chimney at home o’my own pasting up: there be brave pictures! [To Nightingale] Other manner of pictures than these, friend.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Yet these will serve to pick the pictures out o’your pockets, you shall see.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: So I heard ’em say. Pray thee, mind him not, fellow: he’ll have an oar in everything.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: It was intended, sir, as if a purse should chance to be cut in my presence now, I may be blameless though — as by the sequel will more plainly appear.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: We shall find that i’the matter. Pray thee, begin.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: To the tune of Pagington’s Pound , sir.

lg.l: [Sings] Fa, la la la, la la la, fa la la la . Nay, I’ll put thee in tune and all! Mine own country dance! Pray thee, begin.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: It is a gentle admonition, you must know, sir, both to the purse-cutter and the purse-bearer.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Not a word more out o’the tune, an thou lov’st me: Fa, la la la, la la la, fa la la la. Come, when?

lg.l: [Sings] My masters and friends, and good people draw near,
And look to your purses, for that I do say ;

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Ha, ha, this chimes! Good counsel at first dash.

l.emph: And though little money in them you do bear,
It cost more to get than to lose in a day

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Good! Good! In Creaser’s edition, this speech is printed fush right at the end of the previous line.

l.emph: You oft have been told,
Both the young and the old,
And bidden beware of the cutpurse so bold:

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well said! He were to blame that would not, i’faith. i’faith. In Creaser’s editioin, this speech is printed in a right-hand column alongside lines “Who both ... thy nurse”.

l.emph: Then if you take heed not, free me from the curse,
Who both give you warning, for and the cutpurse.
Youth, youth, thou hadst better been starved by thy nurse,
Than live to be hangèd for cutting a purse.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Good, i’faith, how say you, Numps? Is there any harm i’this?

l.emph: It hath been upbraided to men of my trade
That oftentimes we are the cause of this crime.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: The more coxcombs they that did it, I wusse. wusse. In Creaser’s edition, this speech is printed in a right-hand column alongisde lines “ That oftentimes ... it be said? ”.

l.emph: Alack and for pity, why should it be said?
As if they regarded or places or time.
Examples have been
Of some that were seen
In Westminster Hall, yea the pleaders between.
Then why should the judges be free from this curse
More than my poor self, for cutting the purse?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: God-a-mercy for that! Why should they be more free, indeed? indeed? In Creaser’s edition, this speech is printed in a right-hand column alongside lines “ Then why ... thy nurse, ”.

l.emph: Youth, youth, thou hadst better been starved by thy nurse,
Than live to be hangèd for cutting a purse.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: That again, good ballad-man, that again. (He sings the burden with him [as Nightingale repeats it.] ) Oh, rare! I would fain rub mine elbow now, but I dare not pull out my hand. On, I pray thee — he that made this ballad shall be poet to my masque.

l.emph: At Worcester ’tis known well, and even i’the jail,
A knight of good worship did there show his face,
Against the foul sinners in zeal for to rail,
And lost (ipso facto) his purse in the place.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Is it possible? possible? In Creaser’s edition, this speech is printed in a right-hand column parallel to the line “ And lost ... the place ”.

l.emph: Nay, once from the seat
Of judgement so great,
A judge there did lose a fair pouch of velvete.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I'faith? I'faith? In Creaser’s edition, this speech is printed in a right-hand column parallel to the line “ A judge ... velvete. ”.

l.emph: O Lord for thy mercy, how wicked or worse,
Are those that so venture their necks for a purse!
Youth, youth, thou hadst better been starved by thy nurse,
Than live to be hangèd for cutting a purse.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: [Singing along again] Youth, youth, etc! Pray thee, stay a little, friend, yet. — O’thy conscience, Numps, speak, is there any harm i’this?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: To tell you true, ’tis too good for you, ’less you had grace to follow it.

p.seg: It doth discover enormity, I’ll mark it more: I ha’not liked a paltry piece of poetry so well a good while.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: [Singing] Youth, youth, etc! Where’s this youth now? A man must call upon him for his own good, and yet he will not appear. Look here, here’s for him. (He shows his purse.) Handy-dandy, which hand will he have? On, I pray thee, with the rest. I do hear of him, but I cannot see him, this Master Youth, the cutpurse.

l.emph: At plays and at sermons, and at the sessions,
’Tis daily their practice such booty to make.
Yea, under the gallows at executions,
They stick not the stare-abouts’ purses to take.
Nay one without grace,
At a far better place,
At court and in Christmas, before the King’s face.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: That was a fine fellow! I would have him now. now. In Creaser’s edition this speech is printed in a right-hand column alongisde lines “At a far better place ... Alack then for pity, must I bear the curse” in Nightingale’s song.

l.emph: Alack then for pity, must I bear the curse,
That only belongs to the cunning cutpurse?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: But where’s their cunning now, when they should use it? They are all chained now, I warrant you. Youth, youth, thou hadst better, etc. The rat-catcher’s charm! — are all fools and asses to this? A pox on ’em that they will not come! That a man should have such a desire to a thing, and want it.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [To Winwife] Fore God, I’d give half the Fair, an ’twere mine, for a cutpurse for him, to save his longing.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Look you, sister, here, here, where is’t now? Which pocket is’t in, for a wager?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I beseech you leave your wagers, and let him end his matter, an’t may be.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Oh, are you edified, Numps?

p.seg: Indeed, he does interrupt him too much. There Numps spoke to purpose.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Sister, I am an ass! I cannot keep my purse! [He shows it(again.)] On, on, I pray thee, friend.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Will you see sport? Look, there’s a fellow gathers up to him, mark! mark! In Creaser’s edition this speech is printed in a right-hand column alongisde Nightingale’s song.

div2.stage: [As Nightingale sings the next verse,] Edgworth gets up to [Cokes], and tickles him in the ear with a straw twice to draw his hand out of his pocket [first finding a handkerchief and next the purse].

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Good, i’faith! Oh, he has lighted on the wrong pocket. pocket. In Creaser’s edition this speech by Quarlous is printed in a right-hand column alongside Nightingale’s song.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: He has it. ’Fore God, he is a brave fellow; pity he should be detected. detected. In Creaser’s edition this speech by Winwife is printed in a right-hand column alongside Nightingale’s song.

l.emph: But O you vile nation of cutpurses all ,
Relent and repent, and amend and be sound,
And know that you ought not, by honest men’s fall,
Advance your own fortunes, to die above ground,
And though you go gay,
In silks as you may,
It is not the high way to heaven (as they say).
Repent then, repent you, for better, for worse,
And kiss not the gallows for cutting a purse.
Youth, youth, thou hadst better been starved by thy nurse,
Than live to be hangèd for cutting a purse.

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: An excellent ballad! an excellent ballad!

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Friend, let me ha’ the first, let me ha’ the first, I pray you.

div2.stage: [He slips the purse and handkerchief to Nightingale.]

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Pardon me, sir: first come, first served. And I’ll buy the whole bundle, too.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [To Quarlous] That conveyance was better than all, did you see’t? He has given the purse to the ballad singer.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Has he?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Sir, I cry you mercy: I’ll not hinder the poor man’s profit. Pray you, mistake me not.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Sir, I take you for an honest gentleman, if that be mistaking. I met youtoday afore — Ha! humph! O God! My purse is gone, my purse, my purse, etc.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Come, do not make a stir and cry yourself an ass thorough the Fair afore your time.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Why, hast thou it, Numps? Good Numps, how came you by it? I mar’l!

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I pray you, seek some other gamester to play the fool with; you may lose it time enough, for all your Fair-wit.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: By this good hand, glove and all, I ha’ lost it already, if thou hast it not — feel else — and Mistress Grace’s handkerchief, too, out o’the t’other pocket.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why, ’tis well, very well, exceeding pretty and well.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Are you sure you ha’ lost it, sir?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: O God! Yes. As I am an honest man, I had it but e’en now, at ‘Youth, youth’.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: I hope you suspect not me, sir.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Thee? That were a jest indeed! Dost thou think the gentleman is foolish? Where hadst thou hands, I pray thee? Away, ass, away!

p.seg: I shall be beaten again, if I be spied.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Sir, I suspect an odd fellow yonder is stealing away.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Brother, it is the preaching fellow! You shall suspect him. He was at your t’other purse, you know! [Overdo is caught.] Nay, stay, sir, and view the work you ha’ done. An you be beneficed at the gallows and preach there, thank your own handiwork.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Sir, you shall take no pride in your preferment; you shall be silenced quickly.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: What do you mean, sweet buds of gentility?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: To ha’ my pennyworths out on you, bud. No less than two purses a day serve you? I thought you a simple fellow when my man Numps beat you i’the morning, and pitied you —

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: So did I, I’ll be sworn, brother; but now I see he is a lewd and pernicious enormity (as Master Overdo calls him).

p.seg: Mine own words turned upon me, like swords.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Cannot a man’s purse be at quiet for you i’the master’s pocket, but you must entice it forth and debauch it?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Sir, sir, keep your ‘debauch’ and your fine Barthol’mew-terms to yourself, and make as much on ’em as you please. But gi’ me this from you, i’the meantime: I beseech you, see if I can look to this.

div2.stage: [He tries to take the box from Cokes.]

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Why, Numps?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why? Because you are an ass, sir — there’s a reason the shortest way, an you will needs ha’ it. Now you ha’ got the trick of losing, you’d lose your breech, an ’twere loose. I know you, sir: come, deliver. (Wasp takes the licence from him.) You’ll go and crack the vermin you breed now, will you? — ’tis very fine. Will you ha’ the truth on’t? They are such reckless flies as you are, that blow cutpurses abroad in every corner; your foolish having of money makes ’em. An there were no wiser than I, sir, the trade should lie open for you, sir, it should, i’faith, sir. I would teach your wit to come to your head, sir, as well as your land to come into your hand, I assure you, sir.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Alack, good Numps.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nay, gentlemen, never pity me, I am not worth it. Lord send me at home once to Harrow o’the Hill again; if I travel any more, call me Coryate, with all my heart.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Cokes, Mistress Overdo, and Wasp, with Justice Overdo.]

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [To Edgworth] Stay, sir, I must have a word with you in private, do you hear?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: With me, sir? What’s your pleasure, good sir?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Do not deny it: you are a cutpurse, sir. This gentleman here and I saw you — nor do we mean to detect you (though we can sufficiently inform ourselves toward the danger of concealing you), but you must do us a piece of service.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Good gentlemen, do not undo me; I am a civil young man, and but a beginner, indeed.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Sir, your beginning shall bring on your ending, for us. We are no catchpoles nor constables. That you are to undertake is this: you saw the old fellow with the black box here?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: The little old governor, sir?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: That same: I see you have flown him to a mark already. I would ha’ you get away that box from him, and bring it us.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Would you ha’ the box and all, sir? Or only that, that is in’t? I’ll get you that, and leave him the box to play with still — which will be the harder o’the two — because I would gain your worships’ good opinion of me.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: He says well: ’tis the greater mastery, and ’twill make the more sport when ’tis missed.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Ay, and ’twill be the longer a-missing, to draw on the sport.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: But look you do it now, sirrah, and keep your word, or —

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Sir, if ever I break my word with a gentleman, may I never read word at my need. Where shall I find you?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Somewhere i’the Fair hereabouts. Dispatch it quickly. [Exit Edgworth.] I would fain see the careful fool deluded! Of all beasts, I love the serious ass: he that takes pains to be one, and plays the fool with the greatest diligence that can be.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Then you would not choose, sir, but love my guardian, Justice Overdo, who is answerable to that description in every hair of him.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: So I have heard. But how came you, Mistress Wellborn, to be his ward, or have relation to him at first?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Faith, through a common calamity: he bought me, sir; and now he will marry me to his wife’s brother, this wise gentleman that you see, or else I must pay value o’my land.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slid, is there no device of disparagement, or so? Talk with some crafty fellow, some picklock o’the law! Would I had studied a year longer i’the Inns of Court, an’t had been but i’your case.

p.seg: Ay, Master Quarlous, are you proffering?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: You’d bring but little aid, sir.

p.seg: I’ll look to you, i’faith, gamester. — An unfortunate foolish tribe you are fall’n into, lady. I wonder you can endure ’em.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Sir, they that cannot work their fetters off must wear ’em.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: You see what care they have on you, to leave you thus.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Faith, the same they have of themselves, sir. I cannot greatly complain, if this were all the plea I had against ’em.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: ’Tis true! But will you please to withdraw with us a little, and make them think they have lost you. I hope our manners ha’ been such hitherto, and our language, as will give you no cause to doubt yourself in our company.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Sir, I will give myself no cause: I am so secure of mine own manners as I suspect not yours.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Look where John Littlewit comes.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Away, I’ll not be seen by him.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: No, you were not best: he’d tell his mother, the widow.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Heart, what do you mean?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Cry you mercy, is the wind there? Must not the widow be named?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Do you hear, Win, Win?

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: What say you, John?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: While they are paying the reckoning, Win, I’ll tell you a thing, Win: we shall never see any sights i’the Fair, Win, except you long still, Win. Good Win, sweet Win, long to see some hobby-horses, and some drums, and rattles, and dogs, and fine devices, Win: the bull with the five legs, Win, and the great hog. Now you ha’ begun with pig, you may long for anything, Win, and so for my motion, Win.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: But we sha’ not eat o’the bull and the hog, John: how shall I long, then?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Oh, yes, Win! You may long to see as well as to taste, Win: how did the ’pothecary’s wife, Win, that longed to see the anatomy, Win? Or the lady, Win, that desired to spit i’the great lawyer’s mouth after an eloquent pleading? I assure you they longed, Win: good Win, go in, and long.

div2.stage: [John and Win return to the booth.]

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: I think we are rid of our new customer, brother Leatherhead; we shall hear no more of him.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: All the better: let’s pack up all, and be gone before he find us.

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Stay a little, yonder comes a company: it may be we may take some more money.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Sir, I will take your counsel, and cut my hair, and leave vapours: I see that tobacco, and bottle-ale, and pig, and Whit, and very Urs’la herself, is all vanity.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Only pig was not comprehended in my admonition, the rest were. For long hair, it is an ensign of pride, a banner, and the world is full of those banners, very full of banners. And bottle-ale is a drink of Satan’s, a diet-drink of Satan’s, devised to puff us up, and make us swell in this latter age of vanity, as the smoke of tobacco, to keep us in mist and error. But the fleshly woman ( which you call Urs’la) is above all to be avoided, having the marks upon her of the three enemies of man: the World, as being in the Fair; the Devil, as being in the fire; and the Flesh, as being herself.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Brother Zeal-of-the-land, what shall we do? My daughter Win-the-fight is fall’n into her fit of longing again —

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: For more pig? There is no more, is there?

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: — to see some sights i’the Fair.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Sister, let her fly the impurity of the place swiftly, lest she partake of the pitch thereof. Thou art the seat of the Beast, O Smithfield, and I will leave thee. Idolatry peepeth out on every side of thee.

p.seg: An excellent right hypocrite! Now his belly is full, he falls a-railing and kicking, the jade. A very good vapour! I’ll in, and joy Urs’la with telling how her pig works: two and a half he ate to his share. And he has drunk a pailful. He eats with his eyes, as well as his teeth.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: What do you lack, gentlemen? What is’t you buy? Rattles, drums, babies —

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Peace, with thy apocryphal wares, thou profane publican: thy bells, thy dragons, and thy Toby’s dogs. Thy hobby-horse is an idol, a very idol, a fierce and rank idol, and thou the Nebuchadnezzar, the proud Nebuchadnezzar of the Fair, that sett’st it up for children to fall down to and worship.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Cry you mercy, sir, will you buy a fiddle to fill up your noise?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Look, Win, do, look, a God’s name, and save your longing. Here be fine sights.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Ay, child. So you hate ’em, as our Brother Zeal does, you may look on ’em.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Or what do you say to a drum, sir?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: It is the broken belly of the Beast, and thy bellows there are his lungs, andthese pipes are his throat, those feathers are of his tail, and thy rattles the gnashing of his teeth.

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: And what’s my gingerbread, I pray you?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: The provender that pricks him up. Hence with thy basket of popery, thy nest of images, and whole legend of ginger-work.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Sir, if you be not quiet the quicklier, I’ll ha’ you clapped fairlyby the heels for disturbing the Fair.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: The sin of the Fair provokes me, I cannot be silent.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Good Brother Zeal!

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Sir, I’ll make you silent, believe it.

p.seg: I’d give a shilling you could, i’faith, friend.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Sir, give me your shilling — I’ll give you my shop if I do not, and I’ll leave it in pawn with you i’the meantime.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: [Giving the money] A match, i’faith, but do it quickly then.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: (He speaks to the widow.) Hinder me not, woman. — I was moved in spirit, to be here this day in this Fair, this wicked and foul Fair — and fitter may it be called a Foul than a Fair — to protest against the abuses of it, the foul abuses of it, in regard of the afflicted Saints, that are troubled, very much troubled, exceedingly troubled, with the opening of the merchandise of Babylon again, and the peeping of popery upon the stalls, here, here, in the high places. See you not Goldilocks, the purple strumpet, there in her yellow gown and green sleeves? The profane pipes, the tinkling timbrels? A shop of relics!

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: [Protecting Leatherhead’s wares] Pray you, forbear: I am put in trust with ’em.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: And this idolatrous grove of images, this flasket of idols! which I will pull down —

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: Oh, my ware, my ware, God bless it!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: — in my zeal, and glory to be thus exercised.

div2.stage: LEATHERHEAD enters with OFFICERS [led by POACHER].

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Here he is: pray you, lay hold on his zeal — we cannot sell a whistle, for him, in tune. Stop his noise first!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Thou canst not: ’tis a sanctified noise. I will make a loud and most strong noise, till I have daunted the profane enemy. And for this Cause —

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Sir, here’s no man afraid of you, or your Cause. You shall swear it i’the stocks, sir.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: — I will thrust myself into the stocks, upon the pikes of the land.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: [To Officers] Carry him away.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: What do you mean, wicked men?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Let them alone; I fear them not.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Officers with Busy, followed by Mistress Purecraft.]

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: [To Win] Was not this shilling well ventured, Win, for our liberty? Now we may go play, and see over the Fair where we list ourselves. My mother is gone after him, and let her e’en go, and loose us.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: Yes, John, but I know not what to do.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: For what, Win?

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: For a thing I am ashamed to tell you, i’faith, and ’tis too far to go home.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: I pray thee, be not ashamed, Win. Come, i’faith, thou shall not be ashamed. Is it anything about the hobby-horse-man? An’t be, speak freely.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: Hang him, base bob-chin, I scorn him; no, I have very great what’sha’- call’um, John.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Oh! Is that all, Win? We’ll go back to Captain Jordan, to the pig-woman’s, Win. He’ll help us, or she with a dripping pan, or an old kettle, or something. The poor greasy soul loves you, Win, and, after, we’ll visit the Fair all over, Win, and see my puppet play, Win — you know it’s a fine matter, Win.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: Let’s away: I counselled you to pack up afore, Joan.

sp.speaker: TRASH
sp.p: A pox of his Bedlam purity. He has spoiled half my ware: but the best is, we lose nothing, if we miss our first merchant.

sp.speaker: LEATHERHEAD
sp.p: It shall be hard for him to find or know us when we are translated, Joan.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Leatherhead and Trash with their wares.]
[Enter] TROUBLEALL, BRISTLE, [and] HAGGIS, [followed by OFFICERS with] JUSTICE [OVERDO, accompanied by] COKES.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: My masters, I do make no doubt but you are officers.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: What then, sir?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: And the King’s loving and obedient subjects.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Obedient, friend? Take heed what you speak, I advise you: Oliver Bristle advises you. His loving subjects, we grant you, but not his obedient, at this time, by your leave: we know ourselves a little better than so. We are to command, sir, and such as you are to be obedient. Here’s one of his obedient subjects [Indicating Justice Overdo] going to the stocks, and we’ll make you such another, if you talk.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: You are all wise enough i’your places, I know.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: If you know it, sir, why do you bring it in question?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: I question nothing, pardon me. I do only hope you have warrant for what you do; and so, quit you, and so, multiply you. He goes away again.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: [to officers] What’s he? Bring him up to the stocks there. Why bring you him not up?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: If you have Justice Overdo’s warrant, ’tis well: you are safe. That is the warrant of warrants. I’ll not give this button for any man’s warrant else.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Like enough, sir, but let me tell you: an you play away your buttons thus, you will want ’em ere night, for any store I see about you. You might keep ’em, and save pins, I wusse.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: If you have Justice Overdo’s warrant, ‘tis well: you are safe. That is the warrant of warrants. I’ll not give this button for any man’s warrant else.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Like enough, sir, but let me tell you: and play away your buttons thus, you will want ‘em ere night, for any store I see about you. You might keep ‘em, and save pins, I wusse.

p.seg: What should he be that doth so esteem and advance my warrant? He seems a sober and discreet person! It is a comfort to a good conscience, to be followed with a good fame in his sufferings. The world will have a pretty taste by this how I can bear adversity; and it will beget a kind of reverence toward me hereafter, even from mine enemies, when they shall see I carry my calamity nobly, and that it doth neither break me nor bend me.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: Come, sir, here’s a place for you to preach in. Will you put in your leg?

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: That I will, cheerfully.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: O’my conscience, a seminary! He kisses the stocks.

div2.stage: They put him in the stocks.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well, my masters, I’ll leave him with you. Now I see him bestowed, I’ll go look for my goods, and Numps.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: You may, sir, I warrant you. [Exit Cokes.] [To Officers] Where’s the t’other bawler? Fetch him, too. You shall find ’em both fast enough.

p.seg: In the midst of this tumult, I will yet be the author of mine own rest, and, not minding their fury, sit in the stocks in that calm as shall be able to trouble a triumph.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Do you assure me, upon your words? May I undertake for you, if I be asked the question, that you have this warrant?

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: What’s this fellow, for God’s sake?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Do but show me ‘Adam Overdo’, and I am satisfied. Goes out.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: He is a fellow that is distracted, they say: one Troubleall. He was an officer in the Court of Pie-powders here last year, and put out on his place by Justice Overdo —

p.seg: Ha!

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: — upon which he took an idle conceit, and’s run mad upon’t. So that. ever since he will do nothing but by Justice Overdo’s warrant: he will not eat a crust, nor drink a little, nor make him in his apparel ready. His wife — sir-reverence — cannot get him make his water or shift his shirt without his warrant.

p.seg: If this be true, this is my greatest disaster! How am I bound to satisfy this poor man, that is — of so good a nature to me — out of his wits, where there is no room left for dissembling!

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: If you cannot show me ‘Adam Overdo’, I am in doubt of you: I am afraid you cannot answer it. Goes again.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: Before me, neighbour Bristle, and now I think on’t better, Justice Overdo is a very parantory person.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Oh! are you advised of that? And a severe justicer, by your leave.

p.seg: Do I hear ill o’that side, too?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: He will sit as upright o’the bench, an you mark him, as a candle i’the socket, and give light to the whole court in every business.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: But he will burn blue, and swell like a boil — God bless us — an he be angry.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Ay, and he will be angry, too, when him list, that’s more: and when he is angry, be it right or wrong, he has the law on’s side, ever. Ay, mark that, too.

p.seg: I will be more tender hereafter. I see compassion may become a justice, though it be a weakness, I confess, and nearer a vice than a virtue.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: [To Bristle] Well, take him out o’the stocks again; we’ll go a sure way to work, we’ll ha’ the ace of hearts of our side, if we can.

div2.stage: [Enter] POACHER [and Officers, with] BUSY [followed by Mistress] PURECRAFT.

sp.speaker: POACHER
sp.p: Come, bring him away to his fellow there. — Master Busy, we shall rule your legs, I hope, though we cannot rule your tongue.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: No, minister of darkness, no, thou canst not rule my tongue: my tongue it is mine own, and with it I will both knock and mock down your Barthol’mew- abominations, till you be made a hissing to the neighbour parishes round about.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: [To Poacher] Let him alone; we have devised better upon’t.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: And shall he not into the stocks, then?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: No, mistress, we’ll have ’em both to Justice Overdo, and let him do over ’em as is fitting. Then I and my gossip Haggis and my beadle Poacher are discharged.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Oh, I thank you, blessed, honest men!

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Nay, never thank us, but thank this madman that comes here: he put it in our heads.

div2.stage: [Exeunt the Watchmen and their two prisoners.]

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Is he mad? — Now heaven increase his madness, and bless it, and thank it! — Sir, your poor handmaid thanks you.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Have you a warrant? An you have a warrant, show it.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Yes, I have a warrant out of the Word, to give thanks for removing any scorn intended to the Brethren.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: It is Justice Overdo’s warrant that I look for. If you have not that, keep your word, I’ll keep mine. Quit ye, and multiply ye.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Come away, Nightingale, I pray thee.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Whither go you? Where’s your warrant?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Warrant? For what, sir?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: For what you go about: you know how fit it is. An you have no warrant, bless you, I’ll pray for you, that’s all I can do.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: What means he?

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: A madman that haunts the Fair — do you not know him? It’s marvel he has not more followers after his ragged heels.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Beshrew him, he startled me: I thought he had known of our plot. Guilt’s a terrible thing! — ha’ you prepared the costermonger?

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: Yes, and agreed for his basket of pears; he is at the corner here, ready. And your prize, he comes down sailing that way, all alone, without his protector: he is rid of him, it seems.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Ay, I know; I should ha’ followed his Protectorship for a feat I am to do upon him, but this offered itself so i’the way, I could not let it scape. Here he comes: whistle. Be this sport called ‘Dorring the Dotterel’.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: (Whistles) Wh, wh, wh, wh, etc.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: By this light, I cannot find my gingerbread-wife nor my hobby-horse-man in all the Fair now to ha’ my money again. And I do not know the way out on’t to go home for more. Do you hear, friend, you that whistle: what tune is that you whistle?

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: A new tune I am practising, sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Dost thou know where I dwell, I pray thee? — nay, on with thy tune, I ha’ no such haste for an answer. I’ll practise with thee.

sp.speaker: COSTERMONGER
sp.p: Buy any pears, very fine pears, pears fine! Nightingale sets his foot afore him and he falls, with his basket.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: God’s so! A muss, a muss, a muss, a muss!

sp.speaker: COSTERMONGER
sp.p: Good gentleman, my ware, my ware, I am a poor man. Good sir, my ware.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: Let me hold your sword, sir: it troubles you.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Do, and my cloak, an thou wilt; and my hat, too.

div2.stage: Cokes falls a-scrambling [again] whilst they run away with his things.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: A delicate great boy! Methinks he out-scrambles ’em all. I cannot persuade myself but he goes to grammar school yet, and plays the truant today.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: Would he had another purse to cut, Zekiel.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Purse? A man might cut out his kidneys, I think, and he never feel ’em, he is so earnest at the sport.

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: His soul is halfway out on’s body at the game.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Away, Nightingale: that way.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I think I am furnished for Cathern pears for one undermeal. Gi’ me my cloak.

sp.speaker: COSTERMONGER
sp.p: Good gentleman, give me my ware.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Where’s the fellow I ga’ my cloak to? My cloak! And my hat! Ha! God’s lid, is he gone? Thieves, thieves, help me to cry, gentlemen! He runs out.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Away, costermonger, come to us to Urs’la’s. [Exit Costermonger.] Talk of him to have a soul? Heart! If he have any more than a thing given him instead of salt only to keep him from stinking, I’ll be hanged afore my time, presently. Where should it be, trow? In his blood? He has not so much to’ard it in his whole body as will maintain a good flea. And if he take this course, he will not ha’ so much land left as to rear a calf within this twelvemonth. Was there ever green plover so pulled! That his little overseer had been here now, and been but tall enough, to see him steal pears in exchange for his beaver hat and his cloak thus? I must go find him out next, for his black box and his patent (it seems) he has of his place — which I think the gentleman would have a reversion of, that spoke to me for it so earnestly.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Would I might lose my doublet and hose, too, as I am an honest man, and never stir, if I think there be anything but thieving and cozening i’this whole Fair. Barthol’mew Fair, quoth he: an ever any Barthol’mew had that luck in’t that I have had, I’ll be martyred for him, and in Smithfield, too. I ha’ paid for my pears, a rot on ’em: I’ll keep ’em no longer. (Throws away his pears.) Y ou were choke-pears to me; I had been better ha’ gone to mumchance for you, I wusse. Methinks the Fair should not have used me thus, an ’twere but for my name’s sake: I would not ha’ used a dog o’the name so. Oh, Numps will triumph, now! (TROUBLEALL comes again.) Friend, do you know who I am? Or where I lie? I do not myself, I’ll be sworn. Do but carry me home, and I’ll please thee: I ha’ money enough there. I ha’ lost myself, and my cloak and my hat, and my fine sword, and my sister, and Numps, and Mistress Grace (a gentlewoman that I should ha’ married) and a cut-work handkerchief she ga’ me, and two purses today. And my bargain o’ hobby-horses and gingerbread, which grieves me worst of all.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: By whose warrant, sir, have you done all this?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Warrant? Thou art a wise fellow, indeed. As if a man need a warrant to lose anything with.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Yes, Justice Overdo’s warrant, a man may get and lose with, I’ll stand to’t.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Justice Overdo? Dost thou know him? I lie there: he is my brother-in-law, he married my sister. Pray thee, show me the way — dost thou know the house?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Sir, show me your warrant: I know nothing without a warrant, pardon me.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Why, I warrant thee, come along: thou shalt see I have wrought pillows there, and cambric sheets, and sweet-bags, too. Pray thee, guide me to the house.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Sir, I’ll tell you: go you thither yourself first, alone; tell your worshipful brother your mind; and but bring me three lines of his hand, or his clerk’s, with ‘Adam Overdo’ underneath; here I’ll stay you, I’ll obey you, and I’ll guide you presently.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ’Slid, this is an ass; I ha’ found him. Pox upon me, what do I talking to such a dull fool? Farewell, you are a very coxcomb, do you hear?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: I think I am: if Justice Overdo sign to it, I am, and so we are all; he’ll quit us all, multiply us all.

div2.stage: [The men] enter with their swords drawn.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Gentlemen, this is no way that you take: you do but breed one another trouble and offence, and give me no contentment at all. I am no she that affects to be quarrelled for, or have my name or fortune made the question of men’s swords.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slood, we love you.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: If you both love me, as you pretend, your own reason will tell you but one can enjoy me; and to that point, there leads a directer line than by my infamy, which must follow if you fight. ’Tis true (I have professed it to you ingenuously) that rather than to be yoked with this bridegroom is appointed me, I would take up any husband, almost upon any trust — though subtlety would say to me (I know) he is a fool, and has an estate, and I might govern him, and enjoy a friend beside. But these are not my aims: I must have a husband I can love, or I cannot live with him. I shall ill make one of these politic wives!

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Why, if you can like either of us, lady, say which is he, and the other shall swear instantly to desist.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Content, I accord to that willingly.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Sure you think me a woman of an extreme levity, gentlemen, or a strange fancy, that (meeting you by chance in such a place as this, both at one instant and not yet of two hours’ acquaintance, neither of you deserving afore the other of me) I should so forsake my modesty (though I might affect one more particularly) as to say: This is he, and name him.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Why, wherefore should you not? What should hinder you?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: If you would not give it to my modesty, allow it yet to my wit: give me so much of woman and cunning as not to betray myself impertinently. How can I judge of you so far as to a choice, without knowing you more? You are both equal and alike to me yet, and so indifferently affected by me as each of you might be the man, if the other were away. For you are reasonable creatures, you have understanding and discourse. And if fate send me an understanding husband, I have no fear at all but mine own manners shall make him a good one.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Would I were put forth to making for you then.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: It may be you are: you know not what’s toward you. Will you consent to a motion of mine, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Whatever it be, we’ll presume reasonableness, coming from you.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: And fitness, too.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: I saw one of you buy a pair of tables e’en now.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Yes, here they be, and maiden ones too, unwritten in.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: The fitter for what they may be employed in. You shall write either of you here a word, or a name, what you like best — but of two or three syllables at most; and the next person that comes this way — because destiny has a high hand in business of this nature — I’ll demand which of the two words he or she doth approve; and according to that sentence, fix my resolution and affection, without change.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Agreed, my word is conceived already.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: And mine shall not be long creating after.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: But you shall promise, gentlemen, not to be curious to know which of you it is, is taken; but give me leave to conceal that till you have brought me either home, or where I may safely tender myself —

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Why, that’s but equal.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: We are pleased.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: — because I will bind both your endeavours to work together friendly and jointly, each to the other’s fortune, and have myself fitted with some means to make him that is forsaken a part of amends.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: These conditions are very courteous. Well, my word is out of the Arcadia then: ‘Argalus’.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: And mine out of the play: ‘Palamon’.

div2.stage: [While they are writing in the tables,] TROUBLEALL comes again.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Have you any warrant for this, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS, WINWIFE
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: There must be a warrant had, believe it.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: For what?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: For whatsoever it is, anything indeed, no matter what.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slight, here’s a fine ragged prophet, dropped down i’the nick!

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Heaven quit you, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Nay, stay a little. Good lady, put him to the question.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: You are content, then?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS, WINWIFE
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Sir, here are two names written —

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Is ‘ Justice Overdo’ one?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: How, sir? I pray you, read ’em to yourself — it is for a wager between these gentlemen — and with a stroke or any difference, mark which you approve best.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: They may be both worshipful names for aught I know, mistress, but ‘Adam Overdo’ had been worth three of ’em, I assure you, in this place — that’s in plain English.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: This man amazes me! — I pray you, like one of ’em, sir.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: I do like him there that has the best warrant. Mistress, to save your longing — and multiply him — it may be this. [He marks one of the names.] But I am still for Justice Overdo, that’s my conscience. And quit you. [Exit.]

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Is’t done, lady?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Ay, and strangely as ever I saw! What fellow is this, trow?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: No matter what, a fortune-teller we ha’ made him. Which is’t, which is’t?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Nay, did you not promise not to inquire?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slid, I forgot that, pray you, pardon me. [Enter] EDGWORTH. [To Winwife] Look, here’s our Mercury come: the licence arrives i’the finest time, too! ’Tis but scraping out Cokes his name, and ’tis done.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: How now, lime-twig? Hast thou touched?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Not yet, sir: except you would go with me and see’t, it’s not worth speaking on. The act is nothing without a witness. Yonder he is, your man with the box fall’n into the finest company, and so transported with vapours: they ha’ got in a northern clothier, and one Puppy, a western man that’s come to wrestle before my Lord Mayor anon, and Captain Whit, and one Val Cutting that helps Captain Jordan to roar, a circling boy — with whom your Numps is so taken that you may strip him of his clothes, if you will. I’ll undertake to geld him for you, if you had but a surgeon ready to sear him. And Mistress Justice there is the goodest woman! She does so love ’em all over, in terms of justice, and the style of authority, with her hood upright — that I beseech you come away, gentlemen, and see’t!

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slight, I would not lose it for the Fair. What’ll you do, Ned?

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Why, stay here about for you. Mistress Wellborn must not be seen.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Do so, and find out a priest i’the meantime. I’ll bring the licence. — Lead, which way is’t?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Here, sir, you are o’the backside o’the booth already: you may hear the noise.

div2.stage: [Enter] KNOCKEM, NORDERN, PUPPY, CUTTING, WHIT, [Mistress] OVERDO, [and] WASP.
[Ursula’s booth opens, revealing the characters talking noisily.]

p.seg: Whit, bid Val Cutting continue the vapours for a lift, Whit, for a lift.

sp.speaker: NORDERN
sp.p: I’ll ne mare, I’ll ne mare, the eale’s too meeghty.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: How now, my Galloway-nag, the staggers? Ha! Whit, gi’ him a slit i’the forehead. Cheer up, man — a needle, and thread to stitch his ears! I’d cure him now an I had it, with a little butter and garlic, long pepper and grains. Where’s my horn? I’ll gi’ him a mash presently shall take away this dizziness.

sp.speaker: PUPPY
sp.p: Why, where are you, zurs? Do you vlinch, and leave us i’the zuds, now?

sp.speaker: NORDERN
sp.p: I’ll ne mare, I’s e’en as vull as a paiper’s bag, by my troth, I.

sp.speaker: PUPPY
sp.p: Do my northern cloth zhrink i’the wetting? Ha?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Why, well said, old flea-bitten. Thou’lt never tire, I see.

div2.stage: They fall to their vapours again.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: No, sir, but he may tire, if it please him.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Who told dee sho, that he vuld never teer, man?

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: No matter who told him so, so long as he knows.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Nay, I know nothing, sir, pardon me there.

div2.stage: [Edgworth and Quarlous approach, but stand to one side.]

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: [To Quarlous] They are at it still, sir: this they call vapours.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: He shall not pardon dee, captain, dou shalt not be pardoned. Pre’de, shweet heart, do not pardon him.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: ’Slight, I’ll pardon him, an I list, whosoever says nay to’t.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [To Edgworth] Where’s Numps? I miss him.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why, I say nay to’t.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Oh, there he is!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: To what do you say nay, sir? Here they continue their game of

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: To anything, whatsoever it is, so vapours, which is nonsense: every long as I do not like it. man to oppose the last man that

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Pardon me, little man, dou musht like it spoke, whether it concerned a little. him or no.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: No, he must not like it at all, sir: there you are i’the wrong.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: I tink I be: he musht not like it, indeed.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Nay, then he both must and will like it, sir, for all you.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: If he have reason, he may like it, sir.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: By no meansh, captain, upon reason, he may like nothing upon reason.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I have no reason, nor I will hear of no reason, nor I will look for no reason, and he is an ass that either knows any, or looks for’t, from me.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Yes, in some sense you may have reason, sir.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Ay, in some sense, I care not if I grant you.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Pardon me, thou ougsht to grant him nothing, in no shensh, if dou do love dyshelf, angry man.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why then, I do grant him nothing, and I have no sense.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: ’Tis true, thou hast no sense indeed.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: ’Slid, but I have sense, now I think on’t better, and I will grant him anything, do you see?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: He is i’the right, and does utter a sufficient vapour.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Nay, it is no sufficient vapour, neither, I deny that.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Then it is a sweet vapour.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: It may be a sweet vapour.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nay, it is no sweet vapour neither, sir: it stinks, and I’ll stand to’t.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yes, I tink it dosh shtink, captain. All vapour dosh shtink.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nay, then it does not stink, sir, and it shall not stink.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: By your leave, it may, sir.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Ay, by my leave, it may stink, I know that.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Pardon me, thou knowesht nothing: it cannot, by thy leave, angry man.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: How can it not?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Nay, never question him, for he is i’the right.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yesh, I am i’ de right, I confesh it; so ish de little man, too.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I’ll have nothing confessed that concerns me. I am not i’the right, nor never was i’the right, nor never will be i’the right, while I am in my right mind.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Mind? Why, here’s no man minds you, sir, nor anything else.

sp.speaker: PUPPY
sp.p: [Pressing drink upon Nordern] Vriend, will you mind this that we do?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [To Edgworth] Call you this vapours? This is such belching of quarrel as I never heard. Will you mind your business, sir?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: You shall see, sir.

sp.speaker: NORDERN
sp.p: [To Puppy] I’ll ne maire, my waimb warks too mickle with this auready.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: [Coming forward] Will you take that, Master Wasp, that nobody should mind you?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why? What ha’ you to do? Is’t any matter to you?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: No, but methinks you should not be unminded, though.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nor I wu’ not be, now I think on’t. Do you hear, new acquaintance, does no man mind me, say you?

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Yes, sir, every man here minds you, but how?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nay, I care as little how, as you do. That was not my question.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: No, noting was ty question. Tou art a learned man, and I am a valiant man, i’faith, la: tou shalt speak for me, and I vill fight for tee.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Fight for him, Whit? A gross vapour, he can fight for himself.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: It may be I can, but it may be I wu’ not. How then?

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Why, then you may choose.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why, and I’ll choose whether I’ll choose or no.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: I think you may, and ’tis true; and I allow it for a resolute vapour.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nay, then, I do think you do not think, and it is no resolute vapour.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Yes, in some sort he may allow you.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: In no sort, sir, pardon me, I can allow him nothing. You mistake the vapour.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: He mistakes nothing, sir, in no sort.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yes, I pre dee now, let him mistake.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: A turd i’your teeth, never ‘pre dee’ me, for I will have nothing mistaken.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Turd, ha, turd? a noisome vapour — strike, Whit.
