div2.stage: [Edgworth steals the licence from the box, and exit.]

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Why, gentlemen, why, gentlemen, I charge you upon my authority, conserve the peace! In the King’s name, and my husband’s, put up your weapons! I shall be driven to commit you myself else.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Why do you laugh, sir?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Sir, you’ll allow me my Christian liberty. I may laugh, I hope.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: In some sort you may, and in some sort you may not, sir.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Nay in some sort, sir, he may neither laugh nor hope in this company.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Yes, then he may both laugh and hope in any sort, an’t please him.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Faith, and I will then, for it doth please me exceedingly.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: No exceeding neither, sir.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: No, that vapour is too lofty.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Gentlemen, I do not play well at your game of vapours, I am not very good at it, but —

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Do you hear, sir? I would speak with you in circle?

div2.stage: He draws a circle on the ground.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: In circle, sir? What would you with me in circle?

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Can you lend me a piece, a Jacobus, in circle?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Slid, your circle will prove more costly than your vapours, then. Sir, no, I lend you none.

sp.speaker: CUTTING
sp.p: Your beard’s not well turned up, sir.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: How, rascal? Are you playing with my beard? I’ll break circle with you.

sp.speaker: PUPPY, NORDERN
sp.p: Gentlemen, gentlemen!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Gather up, Whit, gather up, Whit, good vapours.

div2.stage: [Knockem and Whit steal and hide the cloaks discarded in the fighting, and exeunt.]

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: What mean you? Are you rebels? Gentlemen! Shall I send out a sergeant-at-arms or a Writ o’ Rebellion against you? I’ll commit you, upon my womanhood, for a riot, upon my justicehood, if you persist.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Upon your justicehood? Marry, shite o’your hood! You’ll commit? Spoke like a true justice of peace’s wife, indeed, and a fine female lawyer! Turd i’your teeth for a fee now.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Why, Numps, in Master Overdo’s name, I charge you.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Good Mistress Underdo, hold your tongue.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Alas! poor Numps.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Alas! And why ‘alas’ from you, I beseech you? Or why ‘poor Numps’, Goody Rich? Am I come to be pitied by your tuftaffeta now? Why, mistress, I knew Adam the clerk, your husband, when he was Adam scrivener and writ for twopence a sheet, as high as he bears his head now, or you your hood, dame. (The WATCH comes in [led by BRISTLE and followed by WHIT].) What are you, sir?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: We be men, and no infidels. What is the matter here, and the noises? Can you tell?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Heart, what ha’ you to do? Cannot a man quarrel in quietness, but he must be put out on’t by you? What are you?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Why, we be His Majesty’s watch, sir.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Watch? ’Sblood, you are a sweet watch, indeed. A body would think, an you watched well a-nights, you should be contented to sleep at this time a-day. Get you to your fleas and your flock-beds, you rogues, your kennels, and lie down close.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Down? Yes, we will down, I warrant you: down with him in His Majesty’s name, down, down with him, and carry him away to the pigeon- holes.

div2.stage: [Some of the Watch seize Wasp, and carry him off.]

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: I thank you, honest friends, in the behalf o’the crown and the peace, and in Master Overdo’s name, for suppressing enormities.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: [Indicating Nordern and Puppy, drunk and asleep] Stay, Bristle, here ish anoder brash o’ drunkards, but very quiet, special drunkards, will pay dee five shillings very well. Take ’em to dee, in de graish o’ God: one of ’em does change cloth for ale in the Fair here; te toder ish a strong man, a mighty man, my Lord Mayor’s man, and a wrestler. He has wreshled so long with the bottle here, that the man with the beard hash almosht streeke up hish heelsh.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: ’Slid, the clerk o’the market has been to cry him all the Fair over here, for my lord’s service.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Tere he ish, pre de taik him hensh, and make ty best on him.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Bristle and Watch, with Puppy and Nordern.] How now, woman o’ shilke, vat ailsh ty shweet faish? Art tou melancholy?

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: A little distempered with these enormities. Shall I intreat a courtesy of you, captain?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Entreat a hundred, velvet voman, I vill do it, shpeak out.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: I cannot with modesty speak it out, but —

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: I vill do it, and more, and more, for dee. — [Loudly] What, Urs’la, an’t be, bitch, an’t be, bawd, an’t be!

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: How now, rascal? What roar you for, old pimp?

p.seg: Here, put up de cloaks, Ursh, de purchase. — Pre dee now, shweet Ursh, help dis good brave voman to a jordan, an’t be.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: ’Slid, call your Captain Jordan to her, can you not?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Nay, pre dee leave dy consheits, and bring the velvet woman to de —

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: I bring her, hang her! Heart, must I find a common pot for every punk i’your purlieus?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Oh, good voordsh, Ursh: it ish a guest o’ velvet, i’fait, la.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Let her sell her hood, and buy a sponge, with a pox to her. My vessel is employed, sir. I have but one, and ’tis the bottom of an old bottle. An honest proctor and his wife are at it within. If she’ll stay her time, so.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: As soon ash tou cansht, shwet Ursh. [Exit Ursula into her booth.] Of a valiant man, I tink I am the patientsh man i’the world, or in all Smithfield.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: How now, Whit? Close vapours, stealing your leaps? Covering in corners, ha?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: No, fait, captain, dough tou beesht a vishe man, dy vit is a mile hence, now. I vas procuring a shmall courtesy for a woman of fashion here.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Yes, captain, though I am justice of peace’s wife, I do love men of war and the sons of the sword, when they come before my husband.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Say’st thou so, filly? Thou shalt have a leap presently; I’ll horse thee myself, else.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Come, will you bring her in now, and let her take her turn?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Gramercy, good Ursh, I tank dee.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Master Overdo shall thank her.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Good Gammer Urs, Win and I are exceedingly beholden to you, and to Captain Jordan, and Captain Whit. — Win, I’ll be bold to leave you i’this good company, Win, for half an hour or so, Win, while I go and see how my matter goes forward, and if the puppets be perfect. And then I’ll come and fetch you, Win.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: Will you leave me alone with two men, John?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Ay, they are honest gentlemen, Win — Captain Jordan and Captain Whit— they’ll use you very civilly, Win. God b’w’you, Win.

p.seg: What’s her husband gone?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: On his false gallop, Urs, away.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: An you be right Barthol’mew-birds, now show yourselves so: we are undone for want of fowl i’the Fair here. Here will be Zekiel Edgworth, and three or four gallants with him, at night, and I ha’ neither plover nor quail for ’em. Persuade this between you two to become a bird o’the game, while I work the velvet woman within (as you call her).

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: I conceive thee, Urs! Go thy ways. [Exit Ursula into her booth.] [Speaking to be overheard by Win] Dost thou hear, Whit, is’t not pity my delicate dark chestnut here, with the fine lean head, large forehead, round eyes, even mouth, sharp ears, long neck, thin crest, close withers, plain back, deep sides, short fillets, and full flanks — with a round belly, a plump buttock, large thighs, knit knees, straight legs, short pasterns, smooth hoofs, and short heels — should lead a dull honest woman’s life, that might live the life of a lady?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yes, by my fait and trot, it is, captain. De honesht woman’s life is a scurvy dull life, indeed, la.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: How, sir? Is an honest woman’s life a scurvy life?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yes, fait, shweetheart, believe him: de leefe of a bondwoman! But if dou vilt harken to me, I vill make tee a free woman, and a lady; dou shalt live like a lady, as te captain saish.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Ay, and be honest too sometimes: have her wires and her tires, her green gowns, and velvet petticoats.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Ay, and ride to Ware and Romford i’ dy coash, shee de players, be in love vit ’em; sup vit gallantsh, be drunk, and cost de noting.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Brave vapours!

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: And lie by twenty on ’em, if dou pleash, shweetheart.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: What, and be honest still? That were fine sport.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: ’Tish common, shweetheart, tou mayst do it, by my hand. It shall be justified to ty husband’s faish now: tou shalt be as honesht as the skin between his hornsh, la!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Yes, and wear a dressing, top and topgallant, to compare with e’er a husband on ’em all for a foretop: it is the vapour of spirit in the wife to cuckold nowadays, as it is the vapour of fashion in the husband not to suspect. Your prying cat-eyed citizen is an abominable vapour.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: Lord, what a fool have I been!

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Mend then, and do everyting like a lady hereafter: never know ty husband from another man.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Nor any one man from another, but i’the dark.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Ay, and then it ish no dishgrash to know any man.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: [Within her booth] Help, help, here!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: How now? What vapour’s there?

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Oh, you are a sweet ranger, and look well to your walks! Yonder is your punk of Turnbull, Ramping Alice, has fall’n upon the poor gentlewoman within, and pulled her hood over her ears and her hair through it.

div2.stage: ALICE enters, beating the Justice’s wife.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Help, help, i’the King’s name!

sp.speaker: ALICE
sp.p: A mischief on you, they are such as you are that undo us, and take our trade from us, with your tuftaffeta haunches!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: How now, Alice!

sp.speaker: ALICE
sp.p: The poor common whores can ha’ no traffic for the privy rich ones: your caps and hoods of velvet call away our customers, and lick the fat from us.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Peace, you foul ramping jade, you —

sp.speaker: ALICE
sp.p: ’Od’s foot, you bawd in grease, are you talking?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Why, Alice, I say!

sp.speaker: ALICE
sp.p: Thou sow of Smithfield, thou!

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Thou tripe of Turnbull!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Cat-a-mountain vapours! Ha!

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: You know where you were tawed lately: both lashed and slashed you were in Bridewell.

sp.speaker: ALICE
sp.p: Ay, by the same token, you rid that week, and broke out the bottom o’the cart, night-tub.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Why, lion face! Ha! Do you know who I am? Shall I tear ruff, slit waistcoat, make rags of petticoat? Ha! Go to, vanish, for fear of vapours. Whit, a kick, Whit, in the parting vapour. [Exit Alice, kicked out by Knockem and Whit.] [To Mistress Overdo] Come, brave woman, take a good heart: thou shalt be a lady, too.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yes, fait, dey shall all both be ladies, and write ‘Madam’. I vill do’t myself for dem: ‘Do’ is the vord, and D is the middle letter of ‘Madam’: D D. Put ’em together and make deeds, without which all words are alike, la.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: ’Tis true, Urs’la. Take ’em in, open thy wardrobe, and fit ’em to their calling. Green gowns, crimson petticoats, green women! My Lord Mayor’s green women! Guests o’the game, true bred. I’ll provide you a coach to take the air in.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: But do you think you can get one?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Oh, they are as common as wheelbarrows where there are great dunghills. Every pettifogger’s wife has ’em, for first he buys a coach that he may marry, and then he marries that he may be made cuckold in’t: for if their wives ride not to their cuckolding, they do ’em no credit. Hide and be hidden; ride and be ridden, says the vapour of experience.

div2.stage: [Exeunt Ursula, Win, and Mistress Overdo into the rear section of the booth.]

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: By what warrant does it say so?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Ha! Mad child o’the Piepowders, art thou there? — [Calling into the booth] Fill us a fresh can, Urs, we may drink together!

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: I may not drink without a warrant, captain.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: ’Slood, thou’ll not stale without a warrant, shortly. Whit, give me pen, ink, and paper: I’ll draw him a warrant presently.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: It must be Justice Overdo’s!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: I know, man. Fetch the drink, Whit.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: I pre dee now, be very brief, captain, for de new ladies stay for dee.

div2.stage: [Exit, returning at once with the drinks and writing materials.]

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: [Writing] Oh, as brief as can be. Here ’tis already: ‘Adam Overdo’.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Why, now I’ll pledge you, captain.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Drink it off. I’ll come to thee anon, again.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: (To the Cutpurse [as he hands over the licence] ) Well, sir. You are now discharged; beware of being spied hereafter.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Sir, will it please you enter in here at Urs’la’s, and take part of a silken gown, a velvet petticoat, or a wrought smock? I am promised such, and I can spare any gentleman a moiety.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Keep it for your companions in beastliness; I am none of ’em, sir. If I had not already forgiven you a greater trespass, or thought you yet worth my beating, I would instruct your manners to whom you made your offers. But go your ways, talk not to me: the hangman is only fit to discourse with you; the hand of beadle is too merciful a punishment for your trade of life. [Exit Edgworth.] I am sorry I employed this fellow, for he thinks me such. Facinus quos inquinat, aequat. But it was for sport. And would I make it serious, the getting of this licence is nothing to me without other circumstances concur. I do think how impertinently I labour if the word be not mine that the ragged fellow marked — and what advantage I have given Ned Winwife in this time now of working her, though it be mine. He’ll go near to form to her what a debauched rascalI am, and fright her out of all good conceit of me — I should do so by him, I am sure, if I had the opportunity. But my hope is in her temper yet — and it must needs be next to despair that is grounded on any part of a woman’s discretion. I would give, by my troth, now, all I could spare ( to my clothes and my sword) to meet my tattered soothsayer again who was my judge i’the question, to know certainly whose word he has damned or saved. For till then, I live but under a reprieve. I must seek him. — Who be these?

div2.stage: Enter WASP with [BRISTLE and some of] the OFFICERS.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Sir, you are a Welsh cuckold, and a prating runt, and no constable.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: You say very well. Come put in his leg in the middle roundel, and let him hole there.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: [As Bristle puts him in the stocks] You stink of leeks, metheglin, and cheese. You rogue!

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Why, what is that to you, if you sit sweetly in the stocks in the meantime? If you have a mind to stink, too, your breeches sit close enough to your bum. Sit you merry, sir.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: How now, Numps?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: It is no matter, how. Pray you, look off.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Nay, I’ll not offend you, Numps. I thought you had sat there to be seen.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: And to be sold, did you not? Pray you, mind your business, an you have any.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Cry you mercy, Numps. Does your leg lie high enough?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: How now, neighbour Haggis, what says Justice Overdo’s Worship to the other offenders?

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: Why, he says just nothing. What should he say? Or where should he say? He is not to be found, man. He ha’ not been seen i’the Fair here all this livelong day, never since seven a’clock i’the morning. His clerks know not what to think on’t. There is no Court of Piepowders yet. — Here they be returned.

div2.stage: [Enter other OFFICERS with] JUSTICE OVERDO [and] BUSY.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: What shall be done with ’em, then, in your discretion?

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: I think we were best put ’em in the stocks, in discretion (there they will be safe, in discretion) for the valour of an hour, or such a thing, till his worship come.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: It is but a hole matter if we do, neighbour Haggis. [To Wasp] Come, sir, here is company for you. [To Haggis] Heave up the stocks.

p.seg: I shall put a trick upon your Welsh diligence, perhaps.

div2.stage: As they open the stocks, Wasp puts his shoe on his hand, and slips it in for his leg.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: [To Busy] Put in your leg, sir.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: What, Rabbi Busy! Is he come?

div2.stage: They bring Busy, and put him in. [When Justice Overdo has also been put in, the Watch stand aside.]

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: I do obey thee: the lion may roar, but he cannot bite. I am glad to be thus separated from the heathen of the land, and put apart in the stocks for the holy Cause.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: What are you, sir?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: One that rejoiceth in his affliction, and sitteth here to prophesy the destruction of fairs and May-games, wakes, and Whitsun ales, and doth sigh and groan for the reformation of these abuses.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: [To Justice Overdo] And do you sigh and groan, too, or rejoice in your affliction?

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: I do not feel it, I do not think of it, it is a thing without me. [To himself] Adam, thou art above these batteries, these contumelies. In te manca ruit fortuna , as thy friend Horace says; thou art one quem neque pauperies, neque mors, neque vincula terrent. And therefore, as another friend of thine says (I think it be thy friend Persius) Non te quaesiveris extra.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [Overhearing] What’s here? A Stoic i’the stocks? The fool is turned philosopher!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Friend, I will leave to communicate my spirit with you if I hear any more of those superstitious relics, those lists of Latin, the very rags of Rome and patches of popery.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Nay, an you begin to quarrel, gentlemen, I’ll leave you. I ha’ paid for quarrelling too lately: look you, a device, but shifting in a hand for a foot. God b’w’you.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Wilt thou then leave thy brethren in tribulation?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: For this once, sir.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Thou art a halting neutral — stay him there, stop him! — that will not endure the heat of persecution!

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: How now, what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: He is fled, he is fled, and dares not sit it out.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: What, has he made an escape, which way? Follow, neighbour Haggis!

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Oh, me! In the stocks! Have the wicked prevailed?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Peace, religious sister, it is my calling, comfort yourself, an extraordinary calling, and done for my better standing, my surer standing, hereafter.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: By whose warrant, by whose warrant, this?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Oh, here’s my man dropped in I looked for!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Ha!

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Oh, good sir, they have set the faithful here to be wondered at, and provided holes for the holy of the land.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Had they warrant for it? Showed they Justice Overdo’s hand? If they had no warrant, they shall answer it.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Sure, you did not lock the stocks sufficiently, neighbour Toby!

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: No! See if you can lock ’em better.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: [Checking the stocks] They are very sufficiently locked, and truly, yet something is in the matter.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: True, your warrant is the matter that is in question. By what warrant?

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: Madman, hold your peace: I will put you in his room else, in the very same hole, do you see?

p.seg: How! Is he a madman?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Show me Justice Overdo’s warrant, I obey you.

sp.speaker: HAGGIS
sp.p: You are a mad fool. Hold your tongue.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: In Justice Overdo’s name, I drink to you, and here’s my warrant.

p.seg: Alas, poor wretch! How it earns my heart for him!

If he be mad, it is in vain to question him. I’ll try, though. — Friend, there was a gentlewoman showed you two names, some hour since: ‘Argalus’ and ‘Palamon’, to mark in a book. Which of ’em was it you marked?

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: I mark no name but ‘Adam Overdo’: that is the name of names. He only is the sufficient magistrate, and that name I reverence: show it me.

p.seg: This fellow’s mad indeed; I am further off now than afore.
I shall not breathe in peace till I have made him some amends.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Well, I will make another use of him, is come in my head: I have a nest of beards in my trunk, one something like his.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: This mad fool has made me that I know not whether I have locked the stocks or no. I think I locked ’em.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Take Adam Overdo in your mind, and fear nothing.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: ’Slid, madness itself, hold thy peace, and take that.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Strikest thou without a warrant? Take thou that. The madman fights with ’em, and they leave open the stocks.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: We are delivered by miracle! Fellow in fetters, let us not refuse the means; this madness was of the spirit. The malice of the enemy hath mocked itself.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Mad do they call him! The world is mad in error, but he is mad in truth. I love him o’the sudden — the cunning man said all true — and shall love him more and more. How well it becomes a man to be mad in truth! Oh, that I might be his yoke-fellow and be mad with him, what a many should we draw to madness in truth with us!

div2.stage: [Exit, following Troubleall.] The Watch, missing them, are affrighted.

sp.speaker: BRISTLE
sp.p: How now! All scaped? Where’s the woman? It is witchcraft! Her velvet hat is a witch, o’my conscience, or my key — t’ one! The madman was a devil, and I am an ass; so bless me, my place, and mine office.

div2.stage: [Enter] LANTERN [LEATHERHEAD, finely dressed], FILCHER, [and] SHARKWELL [with a banner and a drum. They make ready their puppet theatre.]

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Well, luck and Saint Barthol’mew! Out with the sign of our invention, in the name of wit, and do you beat the drum the while! All the foul i’the Fair, I mean all the dirt in Smithfield — that’s one of Master Littlewit’s carwitchets now — will be thrown at our banner today, if the matter does not please the people. Oh, the motions, that I Lantern Leatherhead have given light to i’my time, since my master Pod died! Jerusalem Pod was a master of motions was a stately thing; and so was Nineveh , and before him. The City of Norwich , and Sodom and Gomorrah, with the rising o’the prentices and pulling down the bawdy-houses there upon Shrove Tuesday. But The Gunpowder Plot : there was a get-penny! I have presented that to an eighteen- or twenty-pence audience nine times in an afternoon. Your home-born projects prove ever the best, they are so easy and familiar. They put too much learning i’their things nowadays, and that, I fear, will be the spoil o’this. Littlewit? I say, Micklewit! If not too mickle! — Look to your gathering there, Goodman Filcher.

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: I warrant you, sir.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: An there come any gentlefolks, take twopence apiece, Sharkwell.

sp.speaker: SHARKWELL
sp.p: I warrant you, sir — threepence, an we can.

div2.stage: The JUSTICE comes in like a porter.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: This later disguise I have borrowed of a porter shall carry me out to all my great and good ends, which, however interrupted, were never destroyed in me. Neither is the hour of my severity yet come to reveal myself, wherein cloudlike I will break out in rain and hail, lightning and thunder, upon the head of enormity. Two main works I have to prosecute first: one is to invent some satisfaction for the poor, kind wretch who is out of his wits for my sake, and yonder I see him coming. I will walk aside, and project for it.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: I wonder where Tom Quarlous is, that he returns not. It may be he is struck in here to seek us.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: See, here’s our madman again.

div2.stage: Quarlous in the habit of the madman is mistaken by Mistress Purecraft.

p.seg: I have made myself as like him as his gown and cap will give me leave.

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: [To Quarlous] Sir, I love you, and would be glad to be mad with you in truth.

p.seg: How! My widow in love with a madman?

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Verily, I can be as mad in spirit as you.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: By whose warrant? Leave your canting. [To Grace] Gentlewoman, have I found you? — save ye, quit ye, and multiply ye. (He desires to see the book of Mistress Grace.) Where’s your book? ’Twas a sufficient name I marked, let me see ’t, be not afraid to show ’t me.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: What would you with it, sir?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Mark it again, and again, at your service.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Here it is, sir: this was it you marked.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ‘Palamon’! Fare you well, fare you well.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: How, Palamon!

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Yes, faith, he has discovered it to you now, and therefore ’twere vain to disguise it longer. I am yours, sir, by the benefit of your fortune.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: And you have him, mistress, believe it, that shall never give you cause to repent her benefit, but make you rather to think that in this choice she had both her eyes.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: I desire to put it to no danger of protestation.

p.seg: ‘Palamon’ the word, and Winwife the man!

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: [To Quarlous] Good sir, vouchsafe a yoke-fellow in your madness, shun not one of the sanctified sisters that would draw with you in truth.

p.seg: ‘Palamon’ the word, and Winwife the man!
I must uncover myself unto him or I shall never enjoy him, for all the cunning men’s promises. —

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Stand aside, I’ll answer you presently. (He considers with himself of it.) Why should not I marry this six thousand pound, now I think on’t? And a good trade too, that she has beside, ha? The t’other wench, Winwife is sure of; there’s no expectation for me there! Here I may make myself some saver yet, if she continue mad — there’s the question. It is money that I want: why should I not marry the money, when ’tis offered me? I have a licence and all: it is but razing out one name and putting in another. There’s no playing with a man’s fortune! I am resolved! I were truly mad, an I would not! (He takes her along with him.) Well, come your ways, follow me; an you will be mad, I’ll show you a warrant!

sp.speaker: PURECRAFT
sp.p: Most zealously, it is that I zealously desire.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Sir, let me speak with you.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: By whose warrant?

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: The warrant that you tender and respect so, Justice Overdo’s! I am the man, friend Troubleall, though thus disguised (as the careful magistrate ought) for the good of the republic in the Fair, and the weeding out of enormity. Do you want a house or meat, or drink, or clothes? Speak whatsoever it is, it shall be supplied you. What want you?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Nothing but your warrant.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: My warrant? For what?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: To be gone, sir.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Nay, I pray thee, stay. I am serious, and have not many words, nor much time to exchange with thee. Think what may do thee good.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Your hand and seal will do me a great deal of good — nothing else in the whole Fair that I know.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: If it were to any end, thou shouldst have it willingly.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Why, it will satisfy me — that’s end enough — to look on. An you will not gi’ it me, let me go.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Alas! Thou shalt ha’ it presently; I’ll but step into the scrivener’s hereby, and bring it. Do not go away.

p.seg: Why, this madman’s shape will prove a very fortunate one, I think! Can a ragged robe produce these effects? If this be the wise Justice, and he bring me his hand, I shall go near to make some use on’t. He is come already!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Look thee! Here is my hand and seal, ‘Adam Overdo’. If there be anything to be written above in the paper that thou want’st now or at any time hereafter, think on’t. It is my deed: I deliver it so. Can your friend write?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Her hand for a witness, and all is well.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: With all my heart.

div2.stage: He urgeth Mistress Purecraft [and she signs the deed].

p.seg: Why should not I ha’ the conscience to make this a bond of a thousand pound now, or what I would else?

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: [Handing over the document] Look you, there it is; and I deliver it as my deed again.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [To Mistress Purecraft] Let us now proceed in madness.

div2.stage: He takes her in with him.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Well, my conscience is much eased; I ha’ done my part. Though it doth him no good, yet Adam hath offered satisfaction! The sting is removed from hence. Poor man, he is much altered with his affliction, it has brought himlow! Now for my other work, reducing the young man I have followed so long in love, from the brink of his bane to the centre of safety. Here, or in some such like vain place, I shall be sure to find him. I will wait the good time.

div2.stage: [Enter] SHARKWELL, FILCHER [at the entrance to the puppet theatre; then enter] COKES. The BOYS o’the Fair follow him.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: How now? What’s here to do? Friend, art thou the master of the monuments?

sp.speaker: SHARKWELL
sp.p: ’Tis a motion, an’t please your worship.

p.seg: My fantastical brother-in-law, Master Barthol’mew Cokes!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: A motion, what’s that? (He reads the bill.) ‘The Ancient Modern History of Hero and Leander , otherwise called The Touchstone of True Love , with as true a trial of friendship between Damon and Pythias, two faithful friends o’the Bankside.’ Pretty, i’faith — what’s the meaning on’t? Is’t an interlude? Or what is’t?

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: Yes, sir. Please you come near; we’ll take your money within.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Back with these children; they do so follow me up and down.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: [To Filcher] By your leave, friend.

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: You must pay, sir, an you go in.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Who, I? I perceive thou know’st not me. Call the master o’the motion.

sp.speaker: SHARKWELL
sp.p: What, do you not know the author, fellow Filcher? You must take no money of him; he must come in gratis. Master Littlewit is a voluntary: he is the author.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Peace, speak not too loud: I would not have any notice taken that I am the author till we see how it passes.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Master Littlewit, how dost thou?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Master Cokes! You are exceeding well met. What, in your doublet and hose, without a cloak or a hat?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I would I might never stir, as I am an honest man, and by that fire: I have lost all i’the Fair, and all my acquaintance too. Did’st thou meet anybody that I know, Master Littlewit? My man Numps, or my sister Overdo, or Mistress Grace? Pray thee, Master Littlewit, lend me some money to see the interlude here. I’ll pay thee again, as I am a gentleman. If thou’lt but carry me home, I have money enough there.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Oh, sir, you shall command it. What, will a crown serve you?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I think it will. What do we pay for coming in, fellows?

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: Twopence, sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Twopence? There’s twelvepence, friend. Nay, I am a gallant, as simple as I look now, if you see me with my man about me, and my artillery again.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Your man was i’the stocks e’en now, sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Who, Numps?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Yes, faith.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: For what, i’faith? I am glad o’that — remember to tell me on’t anon; I have enough now! What manner of matter is this, Master Littlewit? What kind of actors ha’ you? Are they good actors?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Pretty youths, sir: all children, both old and young. Here’s the master of ’em —

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: (Leatherhead whispers to Littlewit) Call me not Leatherhead, but Lantern.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: — Master Lantern, that gives light to the business.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: In good time, sir, I would fain see ’em; I would be glad to drink with the young company. Which is the tiring house? LANTERN Troth, sir, our tiring house is somewhat little: we are but beginners yet; pray, pardon us. You cannot go upright in’t.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: No? Not now my hat is off? What would you have done with me, if you had had me feather and all, as I was once today? Ha’ you none of your pretty, impudent boys now, to bring stools, fill tobacco, fetch ale, and beg money, as they have at other houses? Let me see some o’your actors.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Show him ’em, show him ’em, Master Lantern: this is a gentleman that is a favourer of the quality.

p.seg: Ay, the favouring of this licentious quality is the consumption of many a young gentleman — a pernicious enormity.

div2.stage: He brings them out in a basket.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: What, do they live in baskets?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: They do lie in a basket, sir; they are o’the small players.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: These be ‘players minors’, indeed. Do you call these players?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: They are actors, sir, and as good as any, none dispraised, for dumbshows — indeed, I am the mouth of ’em all!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Thy mouth will hold ’em all. I think one tailor would go near to beat all this company with a hand bound behind him.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Ay, and eat ’em all, too, an they were in cake-bread.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I thank you for that, Master Littlewit, a good jest! Which is your Burbage now?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: What mean you by that, sir?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Your best actor: your Field?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Good, i’faith! you are even with me, sir.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: This is he that acts young Leander, sir. He is extremely beloved of the womenkind: they do so affect his action, the green gamesters that come here. And this is lovely Hero; this with the beard, Damon; and this, pretty Pythias; this is the ghost of King Dionysius in the habit of a scrivener, as you shall see anon, at large.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well, they are a civil company; I like ’em for that. They offer not to fleer nor jeer nor break jests, as the great players do. And then, there goes not so much charge to the feasting of ’em, or making ’em drunk, as to the other, by reason of their littleness. Do they use to play perfect? Are they never flustered?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: No, sir. I thank my industry and policy for it; they are as well governed a company, though I say it — And here is young Leander: is as proper an actor of his inches, and shakes his head like an ostler.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: But do you play it according to the printed book? I have read that.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: By no means, sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: No? How then?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: A better way, sir — that is too learned and poetical for our audience: what do they know what Hellespont is, ‘guilty of true love’s blood’? Or what Abydos is, or ‘the other, Sestos hight’?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Thou’rt i’the right: I do not know myself.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: No, I have entreated Master Littlewit to take a little pains to reduce it to a more familiar strain for our people.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: How, I pray thee, good Master Littlewit?

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: It pleases him to make a matter of it, sir. But there is no such matter, I assure you. I have only made it a little easy and modern for the times, sir, that’s all: as, for the Hellespont I imagine our Thames here; and then Leander, I make a dyer’s son about Puddle Wharf and Hero a wench o’the Bankside, who, going over one morning to Old Fish Street, Leander spies her land at Trig Stairs, and falls in love with her. Now do I introduce Cupid, having metamorphosed himself into a drawer, and he strikes Hero in love, with a pint of sherry — and other pretty passages there are o’the friendship that will delight you, sir, and please you of judgement.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I’ll be sworn they shall: I am in love with the actors already, and I’ll be allied to them presently — they respect gentlemen, these fellows. Hero shall be my fairing: but which of my fairings? — le’ me see — i’faith, my fiddle! And Leander my fiddlestick. Then Damon my drum, and Pythias my pipe, and the ghost of Dionysius my hobby-horse. All fitted.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Look, yonder’s your Cokes gotten in among his playfellows; I thought we could not miss him at such a spectacle.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Let him alone. He is so busy, he will never spy us. Cokes is handling the puppets. LANTERN Nay, good sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I warrant thee, I will not hurt her, fellow. What, dost think me uncivil? I pray thee, be not jealous: I am toward a wife.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Well, good Master Lantern, make ready to begin, that I may fetch my wife; and look you be perfect: you undo me else i’my reputation.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: I warrant you, sir, do not you breed too great an expectation of it among your friends: that’s the only hurter of these things.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I’ll stay here, and see; pray thee, let me see.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: How diligent and troublesome he is!

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: The place becomes him, methinks.

p.seg: My ward, Mistress Grace, in the company of a stranger! I doubt I shall be compelled to discover myself before my time!

div2.stage: [Enter] KNOCKEM, WHIT, [and] EDGWORTH [with] Mistress OVERDO [and] WIN. [The women are masked, and showily dressed in green gowns.]

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: Twopence apiece, gentlemen: an excellent motion!

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Shall we have fine fireworks and good vapours?

sp.speaker: SHARKWELL
sp.p: Yes, captain, and waterworks, too.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: I pree dee, take a care o’ dy shmall lady there, Edgworth; I will look to dish tall lady myself.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Welcome, gentlemen, welcome, gentlemen!

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Predee, mashter o’ de monshtersh, help a very sick lady here to a chair to shit in.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Presently, sir.

div2.stage: [The Doorkeepers] bring Mistress Overdo a chair. [She quickly falls asleep.]

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Good fait now, Urs’la’s ale and aqua-vitae ish to blame for’t; shit down, shweetheart, shit down, and shleep a little.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: [To Win] Madam, you are very welcome hither.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Yes, and you shall see very good vapours.

p.seg: Here is my care come!

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: This is a very private house, madam.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Will it please your ladyship sit, madam?

p.seg: They do so all-to-be-madam me, I think they think me a very lady!

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: What else, madam?

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: Must I put off my mask to him?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Oh, by no means.

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: How should my husband know me, then?

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Husband? An idle vapour: he must not know you, nor you him — there’s the true vapour.

p.seg: Yea, I will observe more of this.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Ay, and dat is anoder lady, shweetheart; if dou hasht a mind to ’em, give me twelvepence from tee, and dou shalt have eder-oder on ’em!

p.seg: This will prove my chiefest enormity: I will follow this.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Is not this a finer life, lady, than to be clogged with a husband?

sp.speaker: WIN
sp.p: Yes, a great deal. When will they begin, trow, in the name o’the motion?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: By and by, madam: they stay but for company.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Do you hear, puppet-master, these are tedious vapours! When begin you?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: We stay but for Master Littlewit, the author, who is gone for his wife; and we begin presently.

p.seg: That’s I, that’s I.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: That was you, lady, but now you are no such poor thing.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Hang the author’s wife, a running vapour! Here be ladies will stay for ne’er a Delia o’ ’em all.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: But hear me now, here ish one o’ de ladish ashleep. Stay till she but vake, man.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: How now, friends? What’s here to do?

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: Twopence apiece, sir: the best motion in the Fair.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I believe you lie. If you do, I’ll have my money again, and beat you.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Numps is come!

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Did you see a master of mine come in here: a tall young squire of Harrow o’the Hill, Master Barthol’mew Cokes?

sp.speaker: FILCHER
sp.p: I think there be such a one within.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Look he be: you were best — but it is very likely. I wonder I found him not at all the rest. I ha’ been at the eagle, and the black wolf, and the bull with the five legs and two pizzles — he was a calf at Uxbridge Fair two years agone — and at the dogs that dance the morris, and the hare o’the taber, and missed him at all these! Sure this must needs be some fine sight that holds him so, if it have him.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Come, come, are you ready now?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Presently, sir.

p.seg: Hoyday, he’s at work in his doublet and hose.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Hold your peace, Numps: you ha’ been i’the stocks, I hear.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: [To himself] Does he know that? Nay, then the date of my authority is out; I must think no longer to reign; my government is at an end. He that will correct another must want fault in himself.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [Overhearing] Sententious Numps! I never heard so much from him before.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Sure, Master Littlewit will not come. Please you take your place, sir; we’ll begin.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: I pray thee, do: mine ears long to be at it, and my eyes, too. — Oh, Numps, i’the stocks, Numps? Where’s your sword, Numps?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I pray you, intend your game, sir; let me alone.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well then, we are quit for all. Come, sit down, Numps; I’ll interpret to thee. Did you see Mistress Grace? — it’s no matter neither, now I think on’t; tell me anon.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [To Grace] A great deal of love and care he expresses.

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: Alas! Would you have him to express more than he has? That were tyranny.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Peace, ho; now, now.

l.emph: Gentles, that no longer your expectations may wander,
Behold our chief actor, amorous Leander,
With a great deal of cloth lapped about him like a scarf,
For he yet serves his father, a dyer at Puddle Wharf,
Which place we’ll make bold with to call it our Abydos,
As the Bankside is our Sestos, and let it not be denied us.
Now, as he is beating to make the dye take the fuller,
Who chances to come by but fair Hero in a sculler?
And, seeing Leander’s naked leg and goodly calf,
Cast at him from the boat a sheep’s eye and a half.
Now she is landed and the sculler come back;
By and by you shall see what Leander doth lack.
Cole, Cole, old Cole!
That is the sculler’s name without control.
Cole, Cole, I say, Cole!
We do hear you.
Old Cole!
Old coal? Is the dyer turned collier? How do you sell?
A pox o’your manners, kiss my hole here, and smell.
‘Kiss your hole, and smell’? There’s manners indeed.
Why, Cole, I say, Cole!
It’s the sculler you need!
Ay, and be hanged.
Be hanged? Look you yonder,
Old Cole, you must go hang with Master Leander.
Where is he?
Here, Cole, what fairest of fairs
Was that fare that thou landedst but now a’ Trig Stairs?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: What was that, fellow? Pray thee, tell me: I scarce understand ’em.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Leander does ask, sir, what fairest of fairs, Was the fare that he landed but now at Trig Stairs?

l.emph: It is lovely Hero.
Nero?
No, Hero.
It is Hero
Of the Bankside, he saith — to tell you truth without erring —
Is come over into Fish Street to eat some fresh herring.
Leander says no more, but as fast as he can,
Gets on all his best clothes, and will after to the Swan.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Most admirable good, is’t not?

l.emph: Stay, sculler.
What say you?
You must stay for Leander,
And carry him to the wench.
You rogue, I am no pander.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: He says he is no pander. ’Tis a fine language; I understand it now.

l.emph: Are you no pander, Goodman Cole? Here’s no man says you are.
You’ll grow a hot Cole, it seems. Pray you, stay for your fare.
Will he come away?
What do you say?
I’d ha’ him come away.
Would you ha’ Leander come away? Why, pray, sir, stay.
You are angry, Goodman Cole; I believe the fair maid
Came over w’ you a’ trust — tell us, sculler, are you paid?
Yes, Goodman Hogrubber o’ Pict-hatch.
How, Hogrubber o’ Pict-hatch?
Ay, Hogrubber o’ Pict-hatch.
Take you that.
The puppet strikes him over the pate.
Oh, my head!
Harm watch, harm catch.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ‘Harm watch, harm catch’, he says — very good, i’faith. The sculler had like to ha’ knocked you, sirrah.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Yes, but that his fare called him away.

l.emph: Row apace, row apace, row, row, row, row, row.
You are knavishly loaden, sculler: take heed where you go.
Knave i’your face, Goodman Rogue.
Row, row, row, row, row, row.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: He said ‘knave i’your face’, friend.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Ay, sir, I heard him. But there’s no talking to these watermen: they will ha’ the last word.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: God’s my life! I am not allied to the sculler yet: he shall be ‘Dauphin my boy’. But my fiddlestick does fiddle in and out too much. I pray thee, speak to him on’t: tell him I would have him tarry in my sight more.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: I pray you, be content; you’ll have enough on him, sir.

l.emph: Now, gentles, I take it here is none of you so stupid
But that you have heard of a little god of love, called Cupid,
Who out of kindness to Leander, hearing he but saw her
This present day and hour , doth turn himself to a drawer.
And because he would have their first meeting to be merry,
He strikes Hero in love to him with a pint of sherry,
Which he tells her from amorous Leander is sent her,
Who after him into the room of Hero doth venter.

div2.stage: Puppet Leander goes into Mistress Hero’s room.

l.emph: A pint of sack, score a pint of sack i’the Coney.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Sack? You said but e’en now it should be sherry.

l.emph: Why so it is: sherry, sherry, sherry.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ‘Sherry, sherry, sherry’! By my troth he makes me merry. I must have a name for Cupid, too. Let me see — thou mightst help me now, an thou wouldest, Numps, at a dead lift, but thou art dreaming o’the stocks still! Do not think on’t, I have forgot it: ’tis but a nine days’ wonder, man; let it not trouble thee.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I would the stocks were about your neck, sir, condition I hung by the heels in them, till the wonder were off from you, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well said, resolute Numps. — But hark you, friend, where is the friendship all this while between my drum, Damon, and my pipe, Pythias?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: You shall see by and by, sir.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: You think my hobby-horse is forgotten, too; no, I’ll see ’em all enact before I go; I shall not know which to love best, else.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: This gallant has interrupting vapours, troublesome vapours. Whit, puff with him.

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: No, I pre dee, captain, let him alone. He is a child, i’faith, la.

l.emph: Now, gentles, to the friends, who in number are two,
And lodged in that alehouse in which fair Hero does do.
Damon (for some kindness done him the last week)
Is come fair Hero in Fish Street this morning to seek:
Pythias does smell the knavery of the meeting,
And now you shall see their true friendly greeting.
You whoremasterly slave, you.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ‘Whoremasterly slave, you’? Very friendly and familiar, that.

l.emph: Whoremaster i’thy face,
Thou hast lain with her thyself, I’ll prove’t i’this place.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Damon says Pythias has lain with her himself; he’ll prove’t in this place.

l.emph: They are whoremasters both, sir, that’s a plain case.
You lie like a rogue.
Do I lie like a rogue?
A pimp and a scab.
A pimp and a scab?
I say between you, you have both but one drab.
You lie again.
Do I lie again?
Like a rogue again.
Like a rogue again?
And you are a pimp again.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ‘And you are a pimp again’, he says.

l.emph: And a scab again.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: ‘And a scab again’, he says.

l.emph: And I say again, you are both whoremasters again,
And you have both but one drab again.
Dost thou, dost thou, dost thou?
What, both at once?
Down with him, Damon.
Pink his guts, Pythias.
What, so malicious!
Will ye murder me, masters both, i’mine own house?

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Ho! well acted my drum, well acted my pipe, well acted still!

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Well acted, with all my heart.

l.emph: Hold, hold your hands.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Ay, both your hands, for my sake! For you ha’ both done well.

l.emph: Gramercy, pure Pythias.
Gramercy, dear Damon.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Gramercy to you both, my pipe and my drum.

l.emph: Come now, we’ll together to breakfast to Hero.
’Tis well, you can now go to breakfast to Hero;
You have given me my breakfast, with a ’hone and ’honero.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: How is’t, friend? Ha’ they hurt thee?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Oh, no!

l.emph: Between you and I, sir, we do but make show.
Thus, gentles, you perceive, without any denial,
’Twixt Damon and Pythias here, friendship’s true trial.
Though hourly they quarrel thus, and roar each with other,
They fight you no more than does brother with brother.
But friendly together, at the next man they meet
They let fly their anger, as here you might see’t.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well, we have seen’t, and thou hast felt it, whatsoever thou sayest. What’s next? What’s next?

l.emph: This while young Leander with fair Hero is drinking,
And Hero grown drunk, to any man’s thinking!
Yet was it not three pints of sherry could flaw her,
Till Cupid, distinguished like Jonas the drawer,
From under his apron, where his lechery lurks,
Put love in her sack. Now mark how it works.
O Leander, Leander, my dear, my dear Leander,
I’ll for ever be thy goose, so thou’lt be my gander.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Excellently well said, fiddle: she’ll ever be his goose, so he’ll be her gander —was’t not so?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Yes, sir, but mark his answer now.

l.emph: And sweetest of geese, before I go to bed
I’ll swim o’er the Thames, my goose thee to tread.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Brave! He will swim o’er the Thames and tread his goose tonight, he says.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Ay, peace, sir: they’ll be angry if they hear you eavesdropping, now they are setting their match.

l.emph: But lest the Thames should be dark, my goose, my dear friend,
Let thy window be provided of a candle’s end.
Fear not, my gander: I protest, I should handle
My matters very ill if I had not a whole candle.
Well then, look to’t, and kiss me to boot.
Now, here come the friends again, Pythias and Damon,
And under their cloaks they have of bacon a gammon.

lg.l: Drawer, fill some wine here. LANTERN How, some wine there?

l.emph: There’s company already, sir, pray, forbear!
’Tis Hero.
Yes, but she will not be taken,
After sack and fresh herring, with your Dunmow bacon.
You lie, it’s Westfabian.
If you hold not your peace, you are a coxcomb, I would say.
What’s here? What’s here? Kiss, kiss, upon kiss.
Ay, wherefore should they not? What harm is in this?
’Tis Mistress Hero.
Mistress Hero’s a whore.
Is she a whore? Keep you quiet, or sir knave, out of door.
Knave, out of door?
Yes, knave, out of door.

div2.stage: Here the Puppets quarrel and fall together by the ears.

l.emph: Whore, out of door.
I say, knave, out of door.
I say, whore, out of door.
Yea, so say I, too.
Kiss the whore o’the arse.
Now you ha’ something to do:
You must kiss her o’the arse, she says.
So we will, so we will.
Oh, my haunches, oh, my haunches — hold, hold!
Leander, where art thou? Stand’st thou still like a sot,
And not offer’st to break both their heads with a pot?
See who’s at thine elbow, there! Puppet Jonas and Cupid.
Upon ’em Leander, be not so stupid.
You goat-bearded slave!
You whoremaster knave.
Thou art a whoremaster.
Whoremasters all.
See, Cupid with a word has ta’en up the brawl.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: These be fine vapours!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: By this good day, they fight bravely! Do they not, Numps?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: Yes, they lacked but you to be their second, all this while.

l.emph: This tragical encounter, falling out thus to busy us,
It raises up the ghost of their friend Dionysius:
Not like a monarch, but the master of a school,
In a scrivener’s furred gown, which shows he is no fool,
For therein he hath wit enough to keep himself warm.
O Damon, he cries, and Pythias, what harm
Hath poor Dionysius done you in his grave
That, after his death, you should fall out thus, and rave,
And call amorous Leander whoremaster knave?
I cannot, I will not, I promise you, endure it.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Down with Dagon, down with Dagon! ’Tis I, will no longer endure your profanations.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: What mean you, sir?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: I will remove Dagon there, I say, that idol, that heathenish idol, that remains (as I may say) a beam, a very beam: not a beam of the sun, nor a beam of the moon, nor a beam of a balance, neither a house beam, nor a weaver’s beam, but a beam in the eye, in the eye of the Brethren; a very great beam, an exceeding great beam; such as are your stage-players, rhymers, and morris dancers, who have walked hand in hand in contempt of the Brethren and the Cause; and been borne out by instruments of no mean countenance.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Sir, I present nothing but what is licensed by authority.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Thou art all licence, even licentiousness itself, Shimei!

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: I have the Master of Revels’ hand for’t, sir.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: The Master of Rebels’ hand thou hast: Satan’s! Hold thy peace: thy scurrility shut up thy mouth. Thy profession is damnable, and in pleading for it thou dost plead for Baal. I have long opened my mouth wide and gaped, I have gaped as the oyster for the tide after thy destruction, but cannot compass it by suit or dispute, so that I look for a bickering ere long, and then a battle.

sp.speaker: KNOCKEM
sp.p: Good Banbury-vapours.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Friend, you’d have an ill match on’t, if you bicker with him here. Though he be no man o’the fist, he has friends that will go to cuffs for him. Numps, will not you take our side?

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Sir, it shall not need. In my mind, he offers him a fairer course: to end it by disputation! Hast thou nothing to say for thyself in defence of thy quality?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Faith, sir, I am not well studied in these controversies between the hypocrites and us. But here’s one of my motion, Puppet Dionysius, shall undertake him, and I’ll venture the cause on’t.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Who? My hobby-horse? Will he dispute with him?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Yes, sir, and make a hobby-ass of him, I hope.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: That’s excellent! Indeed he looks like the best scholar of ’em all. — Come, sir, you must be as good as your word now.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: I will not fear to make my spirit and gifts known! Assist me, zeal, fill me, fill me, that is, make me full!

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: [To Grace] What a desperate, profane wretch is this! Is there any ignorance or impudence like his, to call his zeal to fill him against a puppet?

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: I know no fitter match than a puppet to commit with an hypocrite!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: First, I say unto thee, idol, thou hast no calling.

l.emph: You lie, I am called Dionysius.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: The Motion says you lie: he is called Dionysius i’the matter, and to that calling he answers.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: I mean no vocation, idol, no present lawful calling.

l.emph: Is yours a lawful calling?

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: The motion asketh if yours be a lawful calling?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Yes, mine is of the spirit.

l.emph: Then idol is a lawful calling.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: He says, then idol is a lawful calling! For you called him idol, and your calling is of the spirit.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Well disputed, hobby-horse!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Take not part with the wicked, young gallant. He neigheth and hinnyeth; all is but hinnying sophistry. I call him idol again. Yet I say, his calling, his profession, is profane: it is profane, idol.

l.emph: It is not profane!

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: It is not profane, he says.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: It is profane.

l.emph: It is not profane.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: It is profane.

l.emph: It is not profane.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Well said, confute him with ‘not’ still. — You cannot bear him down with your base noise, sir.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Nor he me, with his treble creaking, though he creak like the chariot wheels of Satan. I am zealous for the Cause —

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: As a dog for a bone.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: And I say, it is profane, as being the page of Pride and the waiting-woman of Vanity.

l.emph: Yea? What say you to your tire-women, then? —

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: PUPPET DIONYSIUS
sp.p: — or feather-makers i’the Friars, that are o’your faction of faith? Are not they with their perukes and their puffs, their fans and their huffs, as much pages of Pride and waiters upon Vanity? What say you? What say you? What say you?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: I will not answer for them.

p.emph: Because you cannot, because you cannot. Is a bugle-maker a lawful calling? Or the confect-makers, such you have there? Or your French fashioner? You’d have all the sin within yourselves, would you not? Would you not?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: No, Dagon.

p.emph: What then, Dagonet? Is a puppet worse than these?

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Yes, and my main argument against you is that you are an abomination: for the male among you putteth on the apparel of the female, and the female of the male.

p.emph: You lie, you lie, you lie abominably.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Good, by my troth, he has given him the lie thrice.

p.emph: It is your old stale argument against the players, but it will not hold against the puppets, for we have neither male nor female amongst us. And that thou mayst see if thou wilt, like a malicious purblind zeal as thou art!

div2.stage: The puppet takes up his garment.

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: By my faith, there he has answered you, friend — by plain demonstration.

p.emph: Nay, I’ll prove against ere a rabbin of ’em all that my standing is as lawful as his; that I speak by inspiration as well as he; that I have as little to do with learning as he; and do scorn her helps as much as he.

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: I am confuted; the Cause hath failed me.

sp.speaker: LANTERN
sp.p: Be converted, I pray you, and let the play go on!

sp.speaker: BUSY
sp.p: Let it go on. For I am changed, and will become a beholder with you!

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: That’s brave, i’faith: thou hast carried it away, hobby-horse! On with the play!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Stay, now do I forbid, I — Adam Overdo! Sit still, I charge you.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: What, my brother-i’-law!

sp.speaker: GRACE
sp.p: My wise guardian!

sp.speaker: EDGWORTH
sp.p: Justice Overdo!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: It is time to take enormity by the forehead, and brand it; for I have discovered enough.

div2.stage: [Enter] to them, QUARLOUS (like the madman) [and Mistress] PURECRAFT.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Nay, come, mistress bride. You must do as I do now. You must be mad with me, in truth. [He indicates the deed.] I have here Justice Overdo for it.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Peace, good Troubleall; come hither, and you shall trouble none. I will take the charge of you, and your friend, too. (To the Cutpurse and Mistress Littlewit.) You, also, young man, shall be my care: stand there.

p.seg: Now, mercy upon me.
Would we were away, Whit: these are dangerous vapours! Best fall off with our birds, for fear o’the cage.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Stay, is not my name your terror?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Yesh, faith, man, and it ish for tat we would be gone, man.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: O gentlemen! Did you not see a wife of mine? I ha’ lost my little wife, as I shall be trusted — my little pretty Win. I left her at the great woman’s house in trust yonder, the pig-woman’s, with Captain Jordan and Captain Whit — very good men — and I cannot hear of her. Poor fool, I fear she’s stepped aside. — Mother, did you not see Win?

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: If this grave matron be your mother, sir, stand by her, et digito compesce labellum ; I may perhaps spring a wife for you anon. — Brother Barthol’mew, I am sadly sorry to see you so lightly given and such a disciple of enormity, with your grave governor, Humphrey. But stand you both there in the middle place; I will reprehend you in your course. — Mistress Grace, let me rescue you out of the hands of the stranger.

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Pardon me, sir, I am a kinsman of hers.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Are you so? Of what name, sir?

sp.speaker: WINWIFE
sp.p: Winwife, sir.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Master Winwife? I hope you have won no wife of her, sir. If you have, I will examine the possibility of it at fit leisure. Now, to my enormities: look upon me, O London! and see me, O Smithfield: the Example of Justice and Mirror of Magistrates, the true top of formality and scourge of enormity. Hearken unto my labours, and but observe my discoveries; and compare Hercules with me, if thou dar’st, of old, or Columbus, Magellan, or our countryman Drake, of later times. Stand forth, you weeds of enormity, and spread. (To Busy) First, Rabbi Busy, thou superlunatical hypocrite; (To Lantern) next, thou other extremity, thou profane professor of puppetry, little better than poetry; (To the Horse-corser, and Cutpurse) then thou strong debaucher and seducer of youth: witness this easy and honest young man; (Then Captain Whit, and Mistress Littlewit) now, thou esquire of dames, madams, and twelvepenny ladies; now, my green madam herself, of the price. Let me unmask your ‘Ladyship’.

sp.speaker: JOHN
sp.p: Oh, my wife, my wife, my wife!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Is she your wife? Redde te Harpocratem!

div2.stage: Enter TROUBLEALL [without his gown and hat, and covering himself with a large pan, pursued by] URSULA [and] NIGHTINGALE.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: By your leave, stand by, my masters, be uncovered!

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: Oh, stay him, stay him! Help to cry, Nightingale: my pan, my pan!

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: What’s the matter?

sp.speaker: NIGHTINGALE
sp.p: He has stol’n Gammer Urs’la’s pan.

sp.speaker: TROUBLEALL
sp.p: Yes, and I fear no man but Justice Overdo.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Urs’la? Where is she? (To Ursula and Nightingale.) Oh, the sow of enormity, this! Welcome, stand you there; you, songster, there.

sp.speaker: URSULA
sp.p: An please your worship, I am in no fault: a gentleman stripped him in my booth, and borrowed his gown and his hat, and [Indicating Troubleall] he ran away with my goods here for it.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Then this is the true madman, and (To Quarlous) you are the enormity!

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: [Removing borrowed clothes and false beard] You are i’the right: I am mad but from the gown outward.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Stand you there.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Where you please, sir.

div2.stage: [Waking,] Mistress Overdo is sick, and her husband is silenced.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Oh, lend me a basin, I am sick, I am sick! Where’s Master Overdo? Bridget, call hither my Adam.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: WHIT
sp.p: Dy very own wife, i’fait, worshipful Adam.

sp.speaker: MRS OVERDO
sp.p: Will not my Adam come at me? Shall I see him no more then?

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Sir, why do you not go on with the enormity? Are you oppressed with it? I’ll help you. Hark you, sir, i’your ear: your ‘innocent young man’ you have ta’en such care of all this day is a cutpurse, that hath got all your brother Cokes his things, and helped you to your beating and the stocks. If you have a mind to hang him now, and show him your magistrate’s wit, you may — but I should think it were better recovering the goods, and to save your estimation in pardoning him. I thank you, sir, for the gift of your ward, Mistress Grace: [He shows the deed.] look you, here is your hand and seal, by the way. Master Winwife, give you joy, you are ‘Palamon’, you are possessed o’the gentlewoman, but she must pay me value: here’s warrant for it. And honest madman, there’s thy gown and cap again; I thank thee for my wife. (To the widow) Nay, I can be mad, sweetheart, when I please, still: never fear me. And careful Numps, where’s he? I thank him for my licence.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: ’Tis true, Numps.

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I’ll be hanged then.

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: Look i’your box, Numps. (Wasp misseth the licence) — [To Justice Overdo] Nay, sir, stand not you fixed here like a stake in Finsbury to be shot at, or the whipping-post i’the Fair, but get your wife out o’the air — it will make her worse else. And remember you are but Adam, flesh and blood! — you have your frailty. Forget your other name of Overdo, and invite us all to supper. There you and I will compare our ‘ discoveries’, and drown the memory of all enormity in your bigg’st bowl at home.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: How now, Numps, ha’ you lost it? I warrant, ’twas when thou wert i’the stocks. Why dost not speak?

sp.speaker: WASP
sp.p: I will never speak while I live again, for aught I know.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: Nay, Humphrey, if I be patient, you must be so, too. This pleasant conceited gentleman hath wrought upon my judgement, and prevailed. I pray you, take care of your sick friend, Mistress Alice. And my good friends all —

sp.speaker: QUARLOUS
sp.p: And no ‘enormities’.

sp.speaker: JUSTICE
sp.p: — I invite you home with me to my house to supper. I will have none fear to go along, for my intents are ad correctionem, non ad destructionem; ad aedificandum, non ad diruendum. So, lead on.

sp.speaker: COKES
sp.p: Yes, and bring the actors along: we’ll ha’ the rest o’the play at home!

l.emph: Your Majesty hath seen the play, and you
Can best allow it from your ear and view.
You know the scope of writers, and what store
Of leave is given them, if they take not more
And turn it into licence. You can tell
If we have used that leave you gave us well,
Or whether we to rage or licence break,
Or be profane or make profane men speak.
This is your power to judge, great sir, and not
The envy of a few. Which if we have got,
We value less what their dislike can bring,
If it so happy be, t’have pleased the King.
